THE LILY OF THE VALLEY. - Far from the noisy haunts of men, ' Down in the quiet valley's shade, There blooms a flower of modest mien blooms smell; 1l In spotless robe of white arrayed. the lily of the valley fair ' Sheddingl ta all te ilnoavluny gracefulila ay echarms t hfragrantat excel. The Saviour viewed its lovely form, of its rase beauty mention made, And said, "The king in glory clad -Was not like one of these arrayed." Emblem of spotless purity," It seems a flower of heavenly birth. Liftirg the human heart above The gloom and darkness of this earth.l From thee, fair lily, are may learn Fx life to act a lowly part, And ever shed on those around The fog, ante of a loving heart.
St.
J. G. PICKARSGILL. UTTERANCE.

But what avail inadequate words to touch The innermost of Truth? Shall I essay, Blinded and weak, to point and lead the way, Or grasp a theme for angels overmuch? Yet if it be that something not my own, Some shadow of the Thought to which our schemes And creeds and rituals are uncertain dreams, Is even to my unworthiness made known, I may not hide what yet I scarcely dare To utter, lest on doubtful lips of mine Th.-, real seem false, the fitness less divine. So through the pauses of au inward prayer, I own the faith which seems the simple truth At evening time, as in the dawn of youth. J. G. WHITTLICR.

THE WITCHING .T 1142 OF NlGHT.—Persons who have watched much with sick people at night, or who have been often awake at midnight from any, cause' have noticed an unusual number of noises at that time. In Nevada, an old Ruby Hill miner, who has had 15 years' experience under- ground, says that he has observed one peculiar fact, i that bet-Wean 12 and 2 o'clock (night), if there is a loose stone or bit of earth in the mine it is sure to fall. About this time it seems that everything begins to stir t. and immediately after 11, although the mine has been still as a tomb before, you will hear particles of rock and earth come tumbling down, and if there is a caving piece of ground in the mine it is sure to give way." —"They ought to be doing well in that country, having been so well supplied with men and money from the United Kingdom; that and the unfavourable seasons for the past few years have been the eause of much distress and ruin to many British farmers, and must be much felt by the landowners, especially; so in some of the arable land districts of strong clays And thin surface oohs on chalk, which it is not an easy matter to convert to meadow or pasture land. There has, I think, 'much mischief been done by gamtding and speculation in trade by men without capital, haVing nothing to lose, treating new companies under false 'we- „tepees, , The liquidation law has been a bad business. The depression in agricniture has not been so mina' felt by the tenant farmers in this district aff In many places. In our uplltnils, which arwabout ZOO feet above theievel of the, sea, on tidal waters tbs,land is mostly in grass and small falrtns, and the occupiers depend More on making butter and rear- ing calves than growing grain for sale. Milk, butter,l and raising young stock has been the best business for Some years, grain at a low price being an advantage father than otherwise, by giving cheap feeding stuffs for milk cows and young stock. Rents of land vary from 255. to 40s. per statute acre, not much at the latter price—average about 305.; and tithes from 3s. to 4s. per acre. I have- Seen re- ports in the local papers that some of the landowners ih the lower districts, where the rents are higher, and where the farmers have suffered from potato disease and deficient grain •Crops, have returned a varying percentage, but not very high. It is a great nilstake to require too high rents of good tenants, for as the tenants, unable to meet the rent, become poorer, so will the land get poorer, and the owner of the land is the chief loser probably in the end. It Will, I think, be 'found in a while that 'many farmers, bare emi- grated; others obliged to give up, having lost all; and others, who have some capitalieft, have retired, rather than venture on farther risk at present. The difficulty, it ap- pears to me, will now be to get suitable tenants with suffi- cient capital."—" R.," in the Agricultural Gazette.

Briefly stated, the facts are these, The alas, Mr. ---,-- was astonished one fine morn- ing at bearing from his loving spouse that his cook, bquse- maia, and parionr-maid had each and all given notice to quit his eel rica, the.reasou assigned being that master had pre4ehed a sermon positively alluding to one of the trio who was blessed with that sooqing adjunct todomestic servitude —a "follower." The fqllower had been seen to follow Maria, Jane, Lucy, or whatever was the name of the fair one so greatly blessed, into an adjohling garden,and—here was the sting-11-the reverend employer of the blessed one had preached from the firet verse of the sth chapter of the Song, of Solomon—"I am come into the garden, my sister, my spouse," dm., "which, main, were of course very piseted, and quite a hinsult," said the injured one; "and we all think so," was the unanimous chorus of the offended trio. In vain was any explanation offered; in vain it was pointed out that allusions intended generally should not have been regarded as personal—" Oh no, mam' " was the response. "there could have been no mistakiu of the delusion, as me and my young man was a sitting in the gallery when master was denunciating his discourse from the pulpit."—They all left.

_ Bum= exre Crutzuv.—Some persons live in a perpetual state of fret. The, weatheris always objectionable; the temperature is nevep satisfactory. They have too much to do, and are drivebi tb tiva`tte, or too little, and have no re- sources. If they ar 111, hey know they shall never-got welt; if they are well. they expect soon to be ill. Their daily work is either drudgery, which they'lafe, or so diffi- cult and complete that they cannot execute it. In contrast to these we sometimes Meet with men and women so bright arid cheery that their very presence is a positive pleasure. They discover the 'favourable side of the weather, of their business, of home surroundings, of social relations, even of political aff,tirs. 'They will tell you of, all the pleasant things that happen and give voice to all the joy they feel. Of course they are sometimes armoyed and worried by petty, troubles, but the very effort they make to pass them over silently diminishes their unpleasant effect, upon themselves, and prevents the influence frem extending. , FEMALE EDUCATION IN TEE LAST CENTURT.—Apropos Of female education, here is an extract from a very old Scotch 'paper; the Aberdeen Journal, published in 1750, which gives us some idea of the education young ladies re- ceived at the bokriling selloole of the last century. THE Constitutional Union of England held its first annual meeting in London. on Monday, under the presidency of Sir Stafford llorthcote. the right hon. Baronet said it 'was no use disguising the fact that at the last generapl election the party suffered a heavy defeat. That he ascribed chiefly to the slack condition into which their organisation had been allowed to fall ;' but there was another cause. They were attacked on S. sudden by unscrupulous, and, at the same time, able opponents, who won over large masses of their countrymen by theieeloquent, excited, and plausible declarations. The effect so produced: he believed, was even now passing off, and it was the mission of that Union to educate the people rn those political questions upon which they had been previously unable to form a correct judg- ment. It WAS important that the young men of the party should take a keen interest in the work, in order that they rnight be ready when the time came to enter Parliament I fully instructed•to govern those people whom they would have to rule. They who were in the House of Commons were often advised to take a division or make a-f‘ slashing" nneech, in order to take' an advantage of their opponents. Such a estirse might plimae their adherents, hut it might also imperil ttnnecessarily a bill which might be required and tend to alienates man whose support on another occa- sion would be needed. In acknowledging a vote of thanks, 'Sir Staff )rd said that there was a great responsibility resting upon him, but that Lord Salisbury and he were looking. confidently forward to the time whtnthey would—and soon —mee wider happier ausp,cos,

FP TI elitiii x,:- ~, , NI t THE RIGHT HON.' W. E. C*§SpicE ' , ~__ • ‘, The Parliament that met bn the 31st o ay,' 1859, dia.' persed on the Bth of July, 1865. The general election which followed did. not occasion any very great excitement
thsoughout the country. No burning questions agitated

the minds of men, and there were few contests that at-- tracted any degree of attention. The Oxford election cer- tainly excited the deepest interest, because of the opposi- tion that was offered to the return of Mr. Gladstone by Mr. Gathorne Hardy, an unuonipromising Conservative. The nomination took place on July 13th, the proceedings being conducted in Latin, At the close 0 the „first day's poll Mr. Gladstone was in a minority of six compared with his Op- ponent. Mr. Hardy. On the third day Mr. Gladstone's minority had increased t 0,74, and on the fourth to 230. On the fourtlmlay the numbers were finally declared— Reathoote" 3,236 Hardy' 1,904 Gladstone Mr. Hardy's majority over Mr. Gladstone was 180. The noblest statesman of the Victorian era was thus Tejected . . .

Oxford, not because the residents at the Univereiti had Wet faith in him, but because non-teisident Tories-had become alarmed, perhaps indignant at MS growing Liberalism The ticket systern Of 'voting, by which long distant MA.' S seated quietly in country parsonages or every studying in duity London chambers with horse hair *ike in Japanned Wires at their 'sides,' were enabled .to record ,theii :votes, was the histriment- which 'Smote Mr. Gladirtene 'and thinbled him from his seat. Both parties ;in the State rejoiced over this rejection, though for widely different reasons. The Con- servative party exulted over it as a triumph of Conserva- tive reaction whilerthe Liberal party rejoiced in the con-,, scionsnerial thht ;it was a, most mistaken stroke of Tory `.llolleY. ;.For! though Mr. Gladstone always courageoly acted upon his own convictions so long as he retained is seat for the Oxford University, he must have remained; to tine extent fettered. pa could not altogether shake ',e;iff e but deep and unmistakable; :.iiifinenee which ouch a connection.xnust.vecessarily have,lestercised. Ihr.t once the ties had. been broken Which bound -him and his Alma Mater, Mr. Gladstone must have felt like• a man Who breathes the fresh- mountain air after a close confinement. theerowded street. The Times, in its leader on Mr. Gladstone's defeat, °b- owed, ," The enemies ,of, the University will make the most of her disgrace: It has hitherto been supposed that a learned constituency was to 8003 p., ext4g.4,.ex,ervt. from the vulgar motives of party spirit,. and capable of 'forming a higher estimate of statesmanship than common tradesmen or tenant farmers. It will now stand ,on record that they have deliberately' sacrificed a repPeieritative who combined • the higheet, qualifications, mot and intelledtaal, for :an academical seat, to 'pithy rfloirit and to party 'iinirit alone. Mr- Gladstone's brilliant public career—his great academical • distinctions and literary attainmentes.his very.subtlety and sympathy with ideas for their own sake mark t him. out .yond all living, men for /mike poskinn,„Howeverprogres- •sive in purely secular politicsihe hart everehown himself a staunglaand.devoteci,chotehroan wherever Church doctrinee or ecclesiastical riglate"werNeyoncerned. Henceforth Gladstone will belong to the country, but no longer to the University. These Oxford Anences and traditions which have so deeply cologrefl Wet:views ariLso greatly interfered with his better judg3inerot, Must gradually lose their hold upon lijm.7 T,he Daelk Pews said, " Mr. Gladatone's career as 'altAterunin eertainly not•ber arkeiittsd•tior Mr. ea- thorne Hardy's capacity be enlarged by the number of votes whiph. Tory squires and Tory parsons may inflict upon Lord Derhy's cheerful and fluent inhaltern, or withheld from Lord Palmerston's brilliant colleagne: The late Sir R. Peel Wag bat the chief of a party,runtil admonished by one ostracism he became finally emancipated by another. Then, as now, the statesman who was destined to give up to mankind what was never meant for the 'barren Services of a party, could say to the honest bigots who rejected him:— , .. I ;banish you r; There Is a world elsewhere. Mediocrity will not be turned into genius; honest and gmd- natured insignificance into force, fluency into eloquence if the resident and non-resident Toryism of the University of Oxford should prefer the safe and sound Mr,,Hardy to the illustrious Minister iviintierflt urope enirlet ii 9; whose name ii-aliciusehold Word in every political assembly of the world."- As.soon as it became ray4e' nt that. Arlr.. flidstone would . be defeated at Oxfoid 'irehastened' di:4d o Lancaslifre; where preparations had been made for bringing him forth as a capclidlita for the Soiti Division of th4ciunty. He • entererrthinchesternest Tuesday, and aböut t&ee o'clock in the afternoon itmers'annonsced on 'Change that he wonl .deliver an address to the electors in this Free Trade Hall.' In I a few moments the room was densely crowded by an eager . audienee,,arid When the great statesman arose and said "At last, nay-' friends "I /AM' earn -adriong' you and "—using I an expression, ad& ,hart' become "very., famous and is not r likely to be forgotten—" lam come among you unmuzzleei,": There was no mistaking the shout that arose as soon as these, _ . .

words rang threngh the hall. "It was the expression of a frieniPhant perception i!if the false move Yrlrfch had been made by those who had taken off the muzzle that had hitherto hindered Mr.' Gladstone from giving unreserved utteranise to 'hie Libehd sentiments, and from fully follow- ing out his Liberal instincts.". We can well remember with what conscious pleasure we followed Mr. Gladstone during this electioneering campaign as he performed, the part of a fieieules and a Stein& rolled into one—the Hercules for strength, the Stentor for soundness of lung and voice,—and as we eagerly devoured the, brilliant speeches delivered at Manchester, Liverpool, arid Wigan, how heartily did we thank the prosy Oxford dons and country parsons for thrhst- ing Out this Antreas rind forcing him to touch his mother earth. Never should we have known what a giant he was if the maundering•Dxoniatt doctors had not found him too good for, thern.ene driven hipaintql the wildernees. It was tnereiore a fOrtnnate circumstance for the nation, though a most nnfortunatecircurnstrunie for ' the Conservative party .geperally, that at this critical period the.Oxoalan Tories took off the muzzle from Mr. Gladstone, and severed is which 6,1 hitherto fettered his liberty of speech and action." Cut free from the impediments of a loyal feeling which, like the heavy baggage of the Roman legionary, hindered the onward progress of the man; Mr. Gladstone was the more able to help forward that .Liberal cause to which he had so 'long given his heath The eontest; 'however, for Sohth Lancashire was a severe one, the polling showing the following, result : Egerton (C) ,Turner (C) 8,806 Gladstone (L) 888 Leigh (C) $ 8,4,776 Thompson (L) HeYwood (L) ' The first three were declared duly elected. The part which Mr. Gladstone played on the stage of English politics from 1865 to 1868, during which period he , continued to represent South Lancashire, need not engage I our attention now, inasmuch as we have already touched upon it in our sketches of Lord John Russel L-and Lord Beaconsfield. But in 1868 Mr. Gladstone wars _rejected by Lancashire, who, to the est:Amish:tient of the wheleumuitry, returned eight Conservatives, being the whole otkbe repre- sentatives of the various divisions of the couldyh county once foremost In its Liberalism among the coantdes of Erg. land. Fortunately, Greenwich bail returnee Mr, grjadstone, without expense and without solicitation oe his part; and when it became evident that the decision of the country was decidedly against Disrae7isna, and that a Liberal policy would be supported by a majority of something like 120 in, the new Parliament, the Cabinet of which Mr, Dieraeli was the head at once resigned; and Mr. Gladstone wxs ,sent for to form a new Administration. He had little or, no diffienlty in excreting the task assigned to him, and tints in 1868 the young man who entered the House of Commons as ; the nominee of the Duke of Newcastle, the Duke who asked if he might not do as he liked with his own—wham Mr. James Grant in 1838 thought would never "acquire the reputa- tion of a great statesman,"-now became the Head of a Liberal Government, find the eighth in the order of her Majesty's Prime Ministers. It is common for those who bold opposite opinions ,to those now hold by Mr.Gladetene to charge him with 'neon-, sistency. We admit that with Mr. Gladstone a "change has come o'er the spirit of his dreams." From the youth- ful politician of 1832 to the Statesman of 1868 there were many startling changes and revolutions of thought. He who began public life as "the rising hope of the stern and unbending Tories," in course of time became the Most popular leader of the Liberal Party., Every vaticinatim. made in his youth he had defeated; aehile to many of the most daring hopes of Liberal politicians he had given 'a complete and splendid realisation. But wif have yet to learn that this tea just ground for censure. That a man should change his opinions is not necessarily a. reproach to him. It is only inferior minds that are never open to conviction. Mr. Gladstone has traversed nearly the whole space which separates the opinions of Lord Eldon frOm the opinions of John Bright, but be has traversed this great distance with gradaal step. He has painfully plodded over the grOund Iwhich others have crossed at a leap. There are Statesmen who persistently resist change. 'There are Statesmen who have as consistently and persistently advocated change. IThere are Statesmen who undergo change, and to this class Mr. Gladstone belongs. But change , with, him is due to "the slow and resistless force of conviction." One of the foremost of his compeers eulogised him as always struggling towards the light. Even his enemies feel that the one idea which always inspires him is a conscientious anxiety to do the right thing. None accuse him of being one of the politicians who mistake, as Victor Hugo says, "a weather- cock for a flag." Clearly Mr. Gladstone is another illustra- tion of the truth so well expressed by our Poet Laureate, "That men may rise on stepping stones of their dead selves to higher things."

• nousg LORDS.—mospAr. Prince Leopold their the bath and his -Seat as Duke of Albany. The Lancashire County Justices Bill was read a third time. THE WASTE OF TRE ARMY. The Earl Of GALLOWAY moved that Her Majesty be Prayed to appoint a royal com- mission to inquire into the causes of the "waste of the army" in ,regard to the increase of desertion and to fraudu- lent enlistments.—The Earl of MORLEY, on behalf of the Government, opposed the motion, and said it was obvious that the noble Earl only wanted another opportunity of at- tacking the neve army system. The Governmeht Were most anxious to do 'everything they could to diminish the was' e complained of. After a discussion, in which the Duke of CAMSRIDGE, Lord SALISBURY* and Earl GRANVILLE Wok part, the motion was withdrawn.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNnev. FENIAN CONSPIRATORS IN THE UNITED STATES.—Mr. STANnapn asked the Prime Minister whether any represen- tations had been addresaed to the Government of the United States as to the preparations being made by an organis.ttion in that country for the commission of outrages in different towns in Englancl.—, Mr. GLarrsroNE: I am not precisely aware in what sense it is that my hon. friend refers to " pre- , I:trationsbeing made in,the United States for the commis- sion of outrages in different towns in England." What we are cognisant of there i in the first place the publication of Moiternents through the public Press in connection un- doebtedly with the collection of money which. may pro- tably be directed to de purpoite of giving effect to those inc4tementa. They,are by no meana limitedta,the commis- slop pi", (Wraps indifferent towns in England, but they in Wale particular individuals and give some of them con- siderable prominence, (Laughter.) What I have to say in answer to the question of the hon. member is that we Ificlught it our duty to bring these extraordinary produc- tions to the knowledge of the Government of the United States. (Cheers.) SEARCHING BRITISH VESSELS.—Sir C DUKE, in answer rr.old Bective said the French Government had admitted that the proceedings of • the Leopard in searching British merchantmen twere not warranted, and expressed regret. In 'answer to other questions, he field that communications were still going on with the French Government with regard to the position of M. Roustan. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDA Y. ~, ...MURIA AND TUNIS—EarI GRANVILLE, in reply to a question,. nlade a statement as to the position of affairs in Bulgaria, ,expressing a hope that the political crisis there would be settled locally in a satisfactory way by an agreement between the prince and the people. After some discussion, a motion by Earl DELAWARR for a copy of M. Roustan's circular, promulgating a decree of the Bey of Tunis constituting him, -as French, minister resident, the sole official intermediary between all foreign representa- tives and the Government of Tunis, was negatived. The Tramways (Ireland) Acts Amendment Bill, the Land Tax Commissioners Names Bill, and the Post Office (Land) Bill were read a third time and passed. •

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. NOTICEs.—Mr. LABoUCHERE gave notice of his intention I to subtnita iresolution respecting the Upper House of the Legislature. • THE firrittst. TREATV wrrn TIT/cm—Replying to Lord leasnoren-Cutmcfrur, with reference to our relations with, Tunis, Sir Charles Ditke said M. Roustan was appointed., Foreign Ministee ,to,the Bey of Tunis, and we were not con- cerned in any right of access he might have in that Capacity. As the representative of ,France he had no more right of access thun,,,Mr.• 'Reade• htel.—Mr. CHTLDEnS afterwards made an appeal to Mr. Rylands to withdraw an .amendment of his to the motion fin going into Committee of Supply on Friday night, so that the Government might put down the Army Estimates.—Mr.RVLANDS placed himself unreservedly in the hands of the Government; but expressed a fear that if he withdrew his motion Lord R. Churchill would carry out a threat he had made of bringing forward one in relation to Tunis.—Sir S. SORTITCOTE Indicated approval of the Government's proposal, and with obvious reference to Lord R. Churchill's threatened persistency, remarked that if Mr. Rylands withdrew his motion in accordance with an arrange- ment made in the House, it would be very unusual for some other members to , step into ;he yacant place.—Lord R. CHURCHILL thereupon took the earliest opportunity of inti- mating that, in case the hon. member for Burnley acceded to the request of the Goversmefit, he should certainly bring in his motion with reference to the affairs of Tunis, which he regarded of first-rate importance.—lt was ultimately I arranged that there should he a general debate on the scheme of Army reform at a morning sitting on Friday. The House then went into committee on the Laed Bill, and the sitting was suspended at seven o'clock. , Upon the resumption of the House at nine o'clock, there was an immediate count out. •

• nag LaseD HILL.—The House went into Committee on the Land Bill, and the discussion of Mr. Healy's amendment to abolish the distinction between present and future tehancies in respect to clause 3, was resumed and continued for some time.—Sir S. NORTIICOTE urged that no doubt should be left as to the views of the Government, and Mr. GLADSTONE said that they had no intention of departing from the original assumption of the Bill that there should be a distinction between present and future tenancies, as a means Of returning at some time to freedom of contract. After some further discuesion the amendment was negatived by 301 to 50.—After this the length of the statutory term was discussed, Mr. C. RUSSELL proposing to substitute 31 for 15 year.—Mr. GLADsioNE opposed any change, and Mr. SHAW, while supporting the longer term, admitted that there was much difference of opinion among the Irish -ntembers.—Mr. Ster.uves thought it would be for the interest of the tenant that the term should be five years;• and Mr. A. BALFOUR suggested 10 years—Mr. PARNELL, on the other hand, held that it would have been wiser to fix a long term, even 1,000 years, with power of periodical revision of rent.—ln the end Mr. Russell's proposal was negatived. Subsection 2 of Clause 3, which finds the land- lord deraanding an unfair rent from a gelling "future tenant " a sum equal to ten times the excess, was amended so as to leave it to the Court to determine the amount by which the landlord, by his unfair demand, has deprecated the selling value of the holding. Various amendments were made in the clause, mostly verbal or of a character to amend the drafting; and at the end Mr. GRAY moved an addition to it providing that tenants in arrear may apply to the Court to Ax such sum as it may deem equitable under the circumstancee.—Mr. GLADSTONE characterised it as incongruonarand pointed out that the proper time for raising the question would be later on at the 43rd clause.--Ulti- mately it was withdrawn, Mr. GLADSTONE having taken the opportunity to deny that the consideration he had promised would *be unfavdurable.—Clause 3 was then agreed to, and progress was made with clause 4. HOUSE OF CIOMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. THE LATE ELECTIONS POR CHESHIRE.—Mr. LABOV- CHERE gave notice that on Friday be would ask the Secre- tary of state for War whether his attention has been called to a letter in the Daily News of the 13th inst., signed " Philip H. Sainsbury, late Captainthaot gen an e f thetielusitßtlteyael Cheshire Light Infantry," in which that his father being the chairman of the committees of the Liberal candidates at the late general election both in the city and county (Chester and West Cheshire), and it being well-known that he (his son) was an ardent Liberal, he received an order from his commanding officer, Colonel the Hon. T. G. Cholmondeley, forbidding him to attend political meetings, although this colonel was then himself actually engaged on the committee of the Gonservative candidates, and permitted his adjutant and other Conserva- tive _officers to attend the Conservative meetings, and all through the late bye-election for West ‘Cheshire was prominent in the cause of the Conservative candidate. And whether; if 'upon iuvestigatien these statements are proved to be correct, he will take steps to call upon Colonel Cholmondeley to retire from the service if he be„,as is re- ported, past the age, when according to the regulations he can be retained in the service. unless amexceptional favour be accorded to him? , THE TELEGRAPH CLERKS AND THE GOVERNMENT.—Mr. O'Doterneti complained of the terms of the recent Treasury minute on the agitation of the telegraph clerks, which, he said, held out a threat of suspension of any clerks who were known to be taking part in any extra-official agitation. The bon. member held that this was a breach of the privileges of the House, but the SPEAKER ruled that the minute could only be brought under notice by motion in the usual man- ner, and that there was no ground for claiming precedence for it as a question of privilege. CAPITAL PuNistlmENT.—Mr. J. W. PEASE moved the second reading of the bill for the abolition of capital punishment. SUPPOSED ELOPEMENT AT ISOLTON.—COUSiderabIO gossip • has been occasioned in Bolton by the elopement of two per- sons in good circumstances. In the centre of the town there resides a tradesman who had a wife nearly 40 years of age. They had been married about 20 years, but had never been blessed with offspring. A bachelor, formerly partner in a manufacturing concern, had been very intimate with this .couple, and some time ago he broke up his home in the suburbs and took apartments with them. A fortnight ago this gentleman left town, stating that he was going to South Africa. Late on Monday night, on the tradesman going home from his club, he found his wife also non est. It is said he missed a large suns of money,and discovered a letter from his wife informing him that for the future he should look after herself. It is supposed she has eloped with the bachelor. NEw EXPRESS TRAINS BETWEEN LIVERPOOL AND MANCHESTER AND LONDON.-10 accordance with a requisi- tion presented a few days ago to the directors of the London and North-western Railway Company, it has been decided that from the let of July next an extra train shall leave Liverpool at six 'o'clock p.m., and at Manchester at ti-lA foe Eusten ; and that at. 6-;0 pm., an extra train will be despatched from Euston for Liverpool and Manchester, thus giving an hour to an hoar 'and 'a half extra in the Aspective cities,which will obviate to a great many the necessity of night travelling. Felton Cauftew Scioo—L—Tfigsg.—The annual treat was given to the scholars ,on Tuesday, when a most enjoy- able day was spent at the pretty village of Weaverham. The conveyance of the teachers and children was safely accom- plished in fivagaily,decorated •waggona, which were kindly supplied by Messrs. Thomas Davies, John E. Bate, Ralph Bate, J. and B. Ellison, J. Gleaye, 'Thomas Andrews, and John Molyneux. ' The road from Prodsham to Weaverham is vety pleasant, and with fine weather,' cheerful company, and rural se.enegy, the distance did not seem so great, while the cheering through' the villages of Five Crosses, Kingsley, and Crowton, was heartily given, and gave evidence of the feelings of pleasure with which the young folk take their annnal trip.— The church drum and fife hand, under the leadership of Mr. Barrow, contributed their enlivening strains to the enjoyment of the company. The usual pastimes were provided in a field at Weaverham, kindly lent by Mr. Peter Darlington; and the time-honnured' games M "kiss in the, ring," Sm., dm.,, were well patronised by the gallant and their friends; while athletics were provided for those disposed for active exercise. The restored Parish 'Cburch afforded, a pleasant hoir it° thersztiquirians_i ,Tea having been paitaken of, the return journey was completed about nine o'clock, and all seemed well pleased with the arrangements Which had been made for the day's pleasure.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DROWNING CASE
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DROWNING CASE

AT•WARR INGTON. Mr. H. W. Yates, coroner, held an inquiry at the Golden Lion, Latchford, on Thursday, on the body of Joseph Tay- lor, 8 years of age, son of James Taylor, tanner, 203, Mersey View, Latchford, who was drowned in the canal, near Black-lane turnbridf.Te on Tuesday evening. The police report stated deceased had fallen into the canal whilst playing with a dog on the bank, but from the evidence of a boy who was near the spat, it would appear that deceased was pushed in by a number of boys, who immediately ran away without trying to save him.—The father having identified the body of the deceased, a boy named James Taylor, living at 201, Mersey View, Latchford, no relation of the deceased, said deceased was stood at the end of the turnbridge over the canal spitting into the water, when some Irish boys pushed the bridge, and knocked deceased into the water. Witness was in Black-lane, about 14 or 15 yards away from the bridge, and he beard the splash when deceased fell into the water. Deceased remained on the surface of the Water struggling for a short time, and them jumped up and sank. He did not again rise to the surface. Witness ran and told a boatman, who undressed himself and jumped in the canal. He could not recover the body, and another man named Dooley made an *attempt, but without success. The boys who had pushed • the deceased ran away up the • lane and over the railway when they SAW the deceased in the water. They were big boys, hut witness did not know them. The boat- man tried to catch them but could not.—A Juryman: Did the boatman run after the boys before he tried to rescue the deceased 7—Witness: Yes.—The Juryman : Would the deceased have been saved if the boatman had gone in the water first P.—Witness: The boy bad gone down when the boatman came.—lnspector Proffitt: Did not you tell the policeman that deceased was playing with a dog when he fell in ?—Witness: No. It was another boy.—lnspector Proffitt: Why did not you tell the policeman of this at the time ?—The boy made no answer; and a juryman remarked that he would probably be too excited.—John Smith, a bricklayer, said he was walking from Latcliferd to his home in Mersey-street, Warrington, when he saw a crowd near the turebridge. He went there, and found that two men were grappling for deceased with a boat hook. Their efforts _ . _

lit, rapidly attains intense and devouring rage if fed , by combustible materials. We do believe that neither Government approves of these outbursts of popular passion, but that the Italian equally with 013 French Government is putting forth all its autiat tit/ to stop the, disturbances. There is no reason for suspecting the 'Government of France of a disposition to pick a quarrel with that of Italy, nor the Italian Govern. meat of any settled purpose of making a cassia bali out of the French coup in Tunis. Neither power is prepared to go to war with the other; neither power can afford to do so. Italy is not strong enough to challenge a war with France, in which her very existence as a united nation would be at hazard. Hardly more can France, though the stronger power, venture to brave the probable effects of a war irith Italy, unless she is driven to it by affronts she cannot brook. Implacable enemies of both the Republic of France and of Italian unity are lying in wait, watching for their opportunity, which they hope is coming, of striking a deadly blow at the object of their hate, at a moment when it is engaged in a life-and • death strug- gle with a formidable antagonist. Internal foes threaten 'each nation, as well as external foes. The re-actionary factions in France cannot conceal the avidity with which they hail the prosPect of the Republican Government discrediting itself, or finding itself landed in a quagmire of embarrassment through some false move in its foreignpolicy. A war in which the army of the Republic sustained a casual defeat would give the Bonapartists and Legitimists in France the only chance they can ever expect to get of sup- plantimg the Republic by a revolutionary movement. As to enemies beyond the'frontier—one can conceive how Prince Biemark would chuckle if he could see the French Government recklessly pursuing courses which would 'force the Italians into a position of abiding hostility to the French. And then, in the case of Italy, it is well known that the Papal party in Italy itself, and in France and Germany too, cherishes unceasingly the hope that one day, by the agency of the French military power engaged in an 1 invasion of Italy, the power of the King of Italy may be vanquished; 'ltalian independence and unity may be shattered together; and the temporal sovereignty of the Pope may be re-established upon the ruins of Italian nationality. And albeit the clerical party in France is politically antagonistic to the Republican Government., 'yet that party would ndt scruple in the least to use that Government as the instrument for overthrowing the kingdom of Italy, and would even be Willing to be reconciled to the Republic if that were a condition of the bargain. These censiderations may well have the effect of sobering the judgment of responsible Italian states- men, and of causing them to resist with all their might the fatal impulse of 'the irresponsible Italian populace to precipitate a disastrous conflict with France about such a matter as' the occupation of Tunis. 'lf the' Italians expected some day to acquire Tunis as an appanage to Italy, either by conquest or by 'treaty, no doubt it is provoking to find themselves forestalled by the French. But Italy can do without Tunis, and it would be nothing less than mad- mess to stake the national existenee in a war with France for an object so comparatively worthless to Italy.

THE German Parliament last week passed a measure in which the working classes o/ other countries besides Clermany will take no small interest. The discontentment of the masses in that country has been the chief domestic difficulty with which Prince Bismarck has had to contend. Germany is a powerful country, but it is very poor, and its poverty has resulted in two distinct and serious movements. One portion of the dissatisfied population sea k to improve their positioa by emigrating, whilst another portion being compelled to remain in the old Fatherland look to Socialistic principles for a remedy from this poverty. Prince Bismarck consequently believes that I he is confronted with the great question which con- fr( ut -al the English Parliament in the earlier days of Lord Beaconsfield—the "condition of the people question." The measure passed by the German Par- liament last week is intended as a partial solution of the social problem, with which the governing classes of that country have to concern themselves. A "Compulsory State' 'Working Men's Accident Insur- ance Bill" has been passed, which it is thought will materially influence the condition of the German artizans, and will proportionately r3duce the discon- tent,. which is the fruitful parent of Socialism and crime. Prince Bismarck goes to work in a way very different from that adopted by Mr. Dodson when he brought in the Employers' Liability Act. The Ger- man Government for the purposes of this new law constitutes itself a huge insurance society, to which the workmen and employers contribute according to a fixed scale, workmen paying one-third of the pre- mium and the employers two-thirds. If Prince Bismarck had had his way the poorest class of work- men, those whose earnings are less than 188. per week, would have had their premiums paid by the Govern- ment; bat Parliament detected a pauperis: n g tendency in that proposal, and it was rejected. We cannot think, however, that the Bill as it stands will accomplish anything like as much as its authors ex- pect. To compel an employer to pay insurance premiums for the benefit of his workmen is an illusory process after all, for it is the workman who must pay in the end. His wages will be reduced at least in proportion to the payment which the employer makes on his behalf. But this is Princ3 Bismarck's way of helping the working classes. It is ledieved that he intends trying to carry the principle further by making life insurance ocrnpulsory in the ssme way. That he will thereby do fro% working classes any real service may well be doubted. We feel certain that no State insurance scheme can ever be so beneficial as the voluntary provident societies which have done sugh useful and important work in England, and which have been powerful agents for encouraging the virtues of self-help, independence, and thrift.

We have no doubt that the vote in the House of Commons, on Wednesday, on Mr. Pease's notion to abolish capital punishment represents very fairly the eentiment of the country. Public opinion does not yet appear to be ripe for trying an experiment which many people fear would lessen the safety of human life, and make murder much commoner oven than it is now. Therefore the barbarous system of hanging is to continue a little while longer, and Englwed—the mother of civilisation—is to lag behind younger nations, clinging to this horrible, remnant of the Dark Ages. 'The day will come when the experiment will be tried in this country, and we venture to think ,that the result will be of an encouraging character. . Experience appears to prove that the gallows is not a deterrent, and that the abolition of the death penalty and the substitu- tion of imprisonment for life does Lot diminish the safeguards of the person. If it did there cannot be a doubt that the instinct of self preservation is suf- ficiently strong to cease those countries which have effected the change to return, long ere this, to capital punishment, whereas it is only in one or two instances that they have done se.. This is s question which of necessity hinges upon the safety of society. If the advocates of capital punishment can show that to any appreciable extent people who now refrain from committing murder through fear of tho conse- quences, would, under the changed condition of affairs, run the smaller risk, that would at once end the argument. We have an undoubted right to protect ourselves. Life is far too sacred a possession for any premium in the shape of light and unterrify. tying punishment to be put upon the fearful crime of murder. But, on tho other hand, the execution of the law should not be suffered to degenerate into the mere manifestation of popular vengeance. If fin- prisonment or life will deter murderers as effectually as capital puniehnient, then it appears to us clearly

that we have no 134,4neffe to take the bv. s of mur- derers. There ikS an accumulation of proof in favour of the theory that the one method is no less deter et than the othet. No kind of punishment that can be devised will prevent the crime of murder altogether. So long as human nature and human passions are what they are we fear that life will be taken by the angry, or jealous, or greedy men and women. Cupidity, revenge, the pangs of despised love, a snore of causes will always be operating to nerve the murderer's arm, and urge him to his horrible deeds. The hangman's noose fails to restrain his desperate hand, and the most ardent advocates of capital punishment are compelled to admit that the scaffold as a deterrent agent is mani- festly a failure. It, therefore, appears to ai that the I only question to be discussed is whether its abolition I would or would not result in a greater failure. It is admitted that the present law is indefensible and that judicial tribunals ought to have the power of recog- fusing degrees of murder. The contention is that the death penalty should be reserved Tor the worst eases. No one will dispute but that there ought to be a dis- tinction between the ease, for instance, of a man who outrages and mutilates a child, and that of a poor be- trayed girl who in the hour Of anguish strangles the newly-born offspring of her shame. This has been recommended over and over again, but our law recognises no classification, and aggravated man slaughter and murder with provocation are jumbled together so that it is difficult to tell one from the other, and in dozens of eases the capital sentence is solemnly pronounced when everybody knows it will never be carried into effect. Some rude kind of differentiation is attempted now paray by the recommendation of the I jury and partly by the action of the Home Secretary, but the system is unsatisfactory and anomalous. Then there is the irrevocability of the death penalty to be considered. Once inflicted it can never be un- done. If an innocent man by some strange web of circumstantial evidence is hanged, not all the jadges nor Home Secretaries can undo the mischief. And who can say that such a thing is impossible? Galley and Hebron were within an ace of being hanged, yet the innocence of both has been clearly established. Who then will venture to say that no innocent man- has really been 'executed? Men have gone to the unseen world protesting their innocence, and it is possible that evidence may some day be forthcoming that will prove their protestations to be true. Then again we feel certain that many criminals are acquitted because juries will not take upon themselves 1 the responsibility of giving a verdict that must be I followed by an irrevocable sentence. So it was in the old days when hanging was inflicted for lesser crimes, and criminals emboldened by this carried on their operations at a wholesale rate. When the law was altered, and convictions were more certain, crime was proportiouately reduced, and is it not possible that a similar reedit would follow the abolition of capital punishment for murder? Tut- ting wide the deterrent influence of hanging, not an argument is left in its favour, for however vile a wretch may be, we have no right, save to influence others to take his life. To this vie re enlightened humanity -must come, but the feeling which is feet crowing in that direction <is not yet powerful enough to change the law. Meanwhile something may be done by the establishment of a Court of Criminal Appeal to get rid of the present anomalous system and to relieve the Home Secretary of the serious responsibility of discriminating between cases for the gallows and those for the cells.

DITTON AND TEE FESTIVAL OF CORMS CIIBISTI.—OD. Sunday upwards of 2,000 people were present at the oak- bration of the festival of Corpus Christi, at St. Michael's Catholic Church, Ditton. The precession, in which the students of the college took part, was of a magnificent character.

UNITED METHODIST FERE CHURCH, WIDNES. —The anniversary serraons of the school connected with this church were preached on Sunday by Mr. James ißramwell, of Liverpool. In the afternoon an address was given on Sunday school work by the Rev. J. Billington, of Runcorn. The collections amounted to about £9. WasTAYAN METHODIST SCHOOL AERTVERRART AT WIDNES.—On Saturday the Rev. W. J. Brawn; of London, preached two sermons in Victoria-road chapel on behalf of the Sunday school: In the afternoon Mr. Robert Shaw, of Runcorn, addressed a meeting of scholars, parents, and friends. The collections amounted to the handsome sum of £4l 7s Id.

MBR IMO OF RUNCORN Commiestownas.—A meeting of this body WAS held on Wednesday evening. Dr. Steele pre- sided, and there were also present Messrs. Williams, Handley, Norman, Lyon, Frith, P. Speakman, J. J. Speak- man, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor.) The only business was the consideration of a draft letter to the Local bovernment Board in respect to the surcharges of the auditor. The draft having been ap- proved, the proceedings terminated.

ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN LAD.—On Sunday after- noon, as John Alfred Houghton, aged 11 years, who lives with his uncle in Trentham-street, Runcorn, was returning home from an out-door service conducted by Mr. Shaw, the seamen's missionary, he was seriously hurt. He was pass- ing one of the locks, at what is known as the Bottom Locks, at a time when some of the men had drawn up the paddle before the gates were closed, and he was caught between the two gates and badly crushed in the region of the chest. Hs was carried home and attended by Dr. Robinson.

THE PROPOSED GLYCERINE WORER AT RUNCORN —The name of the French gentleman who has arranged to commence these works is M. Victor Clolus, and we nyder- stand that the process of manufacture will give off no noxious vapour. The new works will be p,,eted at the tim- ber yard at Green Turn, lately occupied by Mr. W. H Kershaw. The adjacent land will also be tusea over, as the works will cover a large a large area. Mr. Clolus manu- factures about three-fifths of all the glycerine made in Europe and America. The " spent " lye has hitherto been run to waste. It consists of a mixture of salt, glycerine, and a small quantity of soda in solution, also gelatine and albu- men. M. Clolus is the patentee of a very successful pro- cess for recovering the glycerine from this solution of "spent" lye. The lye is concentrated by evaporation until the salts contained in it begin to crystalise. rhe liquid is then cooled to free it from gelatine and albumen. It is afterwards made to absorb carbonic acid, until bicar- bonate ef soda is precipitated and separated from the liquor. After the completion of this process, hydrochloric acid or " spirit of SR " is passed into the liquor, so as to convert any carbonate of soda which has escaped separation into chloride of sodium (common salt); this chloride of 1 sodium is separated from the liquor by crystallisation. The liquor then contains glycerine and a little free hydrochloric acid; after f eeing it from the acid the glycerine is purified and concentrated by suitable means. Glycerine is much used, not only in the manufacture of explosive compounds, , but also in the preparation of toilet soaps, also for sweeten- in a sour wines. 'M. Clolus has contracted with Messrs. Hazlehurst and Sons, of Runcorn; Messrs. Goesage and Sons, Widnes; and Messrs. Crosfield and Son, Warrington, for the purchase of their "spent" lye; and we believe also 1 with one or two soapmakers in Liverpool. This gentleman is also establishing a glycerine manufactory in Glasgow. Re already has two works in successful operation in Paris— one at Billancourt, and one at Marseilles. M. Clolus expresses himself much indebted to Mr. J. R. Frith, who rendered him much assistance; and also to Mr. James Craig who acted as interpreter.

DEATH rnom SUNSTROKE.—On Tuesday, Alice Ann Dux- bury, aged 23 years, daughter of John Duxbury, of 21, Gillibrand-street, Darwen, died from sunstroke. Deceased went to Blackpool, and whilst out sailing in a pleasure boat she was seized with sunstroke, and remained unconscious up to the time of her death.

DEATH OF THE CHIEF CONSTABLE OF CHESETRE.— Captain J. W. Arrowsmith, chief constable of Cheshire, died suddenly on Saturday evening, at his resideace, The Elms, bale, Chester, in the 50th year of his age. About a year ago Captain Arrowsmith suffered severely from heart disease, and was laid up for some time, but he rallied, and of late appeased to enjoy good health. On Saturday, he attended to his official duties as usual. At halt-past ten at night, however, he complained of being un- well, and went to bed. He gradually became worse, and ex- pired at twelve o'clock. The decease,i, whilst in the army, served in the Crimea, and afterw trds in India during the mutiny. About clever. years ago, be was appointed deputy head constable of Cheshire, and he succeeded the late *Cap- tain Smith as head constable in February, 1878. Captain Arrowsmith was highly respected by the magistrates of the county and the public generally. He was a most efficient and paingtaking officer, and great credit is due to him far the present high morale of the large constabulary force which he commanded. The deceased has left a widow and eight children. On Wednesday the funeral took place at the Chester cemetery. The procession started from the residence of the deceased, The Elms, Horde-road, at noon, the two sons and other relatives of the deceased attending an mourners. Several gentlemen of the neighbourhood who were unable to attend sent•their carriages, sad among those who attended the ceremony were the mayor of Chester (Mr. C. Prawn), M. A X. Sidchottom. J.P.; Mr. J. Salmon, Mr. G. Dickson, Mr. M. Williams, J.P. ; and Mr. T. Hoggins, ' J.P. There were nine wreaths placed on the coffin, senthy various friends. Lieutenant-Colenel Cope, deputy chief constable, was in charge of a body of police numbering about 120, who headed the procession to the cemetery. The men all attended voluntarily. The divisional superin- tendents present were the following :—Superintendent Meredith (Macclesfield), Superintendent Little (Aitrincham), Superintendent Hindley (Middlewich), Superintendent Williamson (Runcorn), Superintendent Mayo (Nantwich), Superintendent Neylor (Bddisbury), Superintendent Plant (Broaton)1 Superintendent Egerton (Wirral), and Superin- tendent langard (Hyde). Mr. Oldmeadow, chief euperirt- tendent, was also in attendance. The funeral service was conducted by the Rev. J. Godson, curate in charge of St. Michael's. The coffin adorned with several wreaths, in- , eluding one contribute by the members of the force, bore a simple inscription giving the name of the deceased and the date of his death, with his age, 49 years. CAPTURE OF A POACHER AT BURTONWOOD.—George Sefton, an elderly man, was charged at the County Police Court, on Saturday, before Messrs. Artingstall and Bleckly, with trespassing on the, lion. L. Powys land at Burton- wood, in pursuit of rabbits.—P. C. Phillips met the prisoner, who was carrying a bag ott his back and a number of nets in hands, near Bewsey Lodge, Burtonwood, at a quarter to two o'clock on the previous morning. The circumstance looked suspicious, and the officer asked what were the con- tents of the bag. Prisoner replied, "Only a couple of rat bits," whereupon Phillips desired hint to go with him to the lodge, hut prisoner refused, and tried to escape. A struggle ensued, and the prisoner threw the officer, who, however, still held his prisoner, to the ground. Mr. Powys' gamekeeper then opportunely appeared, and the prisoner was conveyed to the lodge. Prisoner had allowed two rabbits to escape during the struggle, but there woe three in the bag. The rabbits were produced alive in a cage, and all the apparatus necessary for catching them From prisoner's "character "sheet it appeared. be many times previously been convicted of once been comilitred to the sessions for trial.- f Chairman remarked that prisoner had batter chaliv his trade.— Prisoner: I will give it hp. Please let me eff.—ln reply to Alderman Burgess, prisoner said he should work in a cotton mill, but his eyesight was very bad.—The Clerk: You can see anich better by night. (Laughter.)—Prisoner was fined 40s. and costs, or in default a month's imprisonment with hajd labour.—The Bench gave an order for the destruction of the nets.

SIIICIDE IN BANN PARK, WARRINGTON.—At the Coopers' Arms, Bewsey-street, Mr. T. W. Barker, deputy coroner, held an inquest on Tuesday, on the body of Thos. Lea, 71 years of age, whe committed suicide on Sunday last. It appeared from the evidence that the deceased lodged at 42, Dailam-lane. Three years ago he lost his wife, and had since been very strange and melancholy. At a quarter-past twelve on Sunday, he was at his daughter's house, when be seemed very low, and left without saying where he was going. P.C. Seed was on duty in the park in the afternoon, and the deceased inquired of him the time about 20 minutes past five. He was afterwards seen sitting on a form near the pond by a girl named Elizabeth Ann Page, who next noticed him in the water. Her screams attracted the atten- tion of William Wilcock, who tried to reach the deceased with the walking stick he had left on the bank, and told him to get hold of it, but deceased took no notice. P.C. Seed then came up, and they succeeded in getting the deceased to the aide by means of the life buoy. He was then insensible, but they tried to bring him round, and succeeded in getting a good deal of water out of him. He was taken to the Infirmary, but on arrival there was found to be dead. In the possession of the deceased was found a pocket book, razor, &a. The pocket book contained the following entry :—" I hope you will put me in my own grave. This is my last day in this world. God bless everybody. I walked the market-place four nights. My son-in-law and my daughter you must pay ray daughter my club money £10" There were also other entries by the deceased sating that he was distracted hi body and soul, and had no comfort anywhere, and that he should drown him- self in the park pond, where they would find him. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased committed shicide during temporary insanity.

Tirs ANNIVERSARY SERMONS were preached at Hill Cliffs chapel, on Sunday afternoon and evening last oy the Rev. John Haslam, of Gildersome, and the collections in aid of the church and school funds realised £35. Stamm CIRCUIT OF TEE Jonozs.—The following are the dates fixed by the judges for holding the summer assizes :—Lord Chief Justice Coleridge and Mr. Justice Lopes, Lancaster, Saturday, July 9: Manchester, Wednes- day, July 13; Liverpool, Tuesday, July 26. Lord Juetice Baggaley, Chester, Saturday, July 23.

, PLautto-Pturtmoma.—The Clerk of the Peace for Lan- cashire reports that pleurolpneumonia has broken out on the farm of Mr. Tattersall, Rawtenstall, and on the farm of Mr. John Platt, of B3rdsley, near Ashton-under-Lyne. The cattle have been slaughtered. There are 2 farms affected in Lancashire.

WEST CHESHIRE ELECTION EXPENSES.—The ex- penses of the unsuccessful Liberal candidate, Mr. Tonkin- son, Wilmington Hall, Tarporley, were £4,745, and those of Mr. Tollemache the Conservative candidate, £3,518. There is a difference of nearly £7OO in the amount paii to Mr. Tomkinson for his agent over that paid by Mr. Tollemache for his, which explains much of the discrepancy in the total.

At a public meeting held on Tuesday at Altrincham much dissatisfaction was expressed at the answer given by the Directors of the Manchester South Junction and Altrincham Railway Company to a memorial which had been presented to them asking for a reduction of fares and the adoption of third-class contract tickets. After a resolution expressing disappointment with the reply had been adopted, it was decided to memoralize the Midland Railway Company to construct a line between Chorlton-cum-Hardy and Bowden, or between Urrnston and Bowdon.

IMPORTANT SALE OP Pawrwas, &c.—The attention of lovers of the beautiful in art, in the form of pictures, is directed to an announcement in Our advertising columns of the sale by auction, by Messrs. Branch and Leete, of Liver- Pool, of the collection of the late John Burton, of Preston. The deceased was well known as a connoisseur in art. The vatious works about to pass under the hammer may, there- fore, be depended upon as choice specimens of the artists to whom they are credited, and the names of these, in both the oil paintings and the water colour drawings, are both numerous and eminent.

THE GUNPOWDER MAGAZINES IN THE MERSEY.—We understand that in consequence of the recent daring Fenian outrages, extra precautions have been taken to guard the magazines which are moored in the Mersey off Bromborough, and which contain something like 400 tons of powder. In the early part of last week her Majesty's gunboat "Cromer" was taken from the Sloyne and anchored between the two magazines, where she remained till Saturday. On that day the revenue cutter " Charlotte" took the place of the "Cromer," which returned to her usual ancorage in the Sloyne. SEQUEL TO AN ELOPEMENT.—WiIIiam Kenyon, of the White Bull, Blackburn, was charged on remand, at Bolton, on Thursday, with stealing two boxes of cigars from Alice Scholes, formerly a confectioner at Blackburn. Frosecu-1 trix's statement was teat prisoner, under the representation that he was single, induced her to elope with him to Bolton. She supplied him with money with wllich to furnish a house, but on afterwards discovering that he was married she removed the goods to a neighbour's house. The pri- soner then left the town, taking with him the cigars andl other articles. The prisoner, who alleged that prosecutrix knew he was married, was committed for trial.—The pri- soner had summoned Richard Scholes, member of the Astley Bridge Local Board, for having by threats compelled him to affix his name to a certain document to be afterwards used as a valuable security. Kenyon was unable to prove the contents of the paper he signed, and the case was dismissed

CITESIEME QUARTEU SESSIONS.—The next General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for this county will be com- menced on Monday next at Chester Castle. After the read- ing of the usual reports the following mo'ions will be considered :—By the Deputy Chairman : To lay before the Conn bye-laws under the Highways and Locomotives Act, 1878, as altered according to suggestions of the Local Government Board; and he will move that the same be adopted and forwarded to the Local Government Board for approval, and that the Clerk of the Veace give the necessary notice. The Chairman or seine member of the Finance Committee will move that the annual salaries of the county coroners for the five years commencing the let of January, 1881, he fixed as follows, namely: Mr. 11. Churton, £5lO (no alteration); Mr. Yates, £386 (decrease of .£21); Mr. Johnson, £407 (increase of £61); Mr. Ridgway, £B5 (in- crease of £10). The Chairman or some other member of the Police Committee will move that a grant be made of £23 Os dd for repairs at Lynim Police Station; also that a grant be made of £24 Os 3d for repairs to the heating appa- ratus attroxton Police Station. Mr. E. Greenall or some other magistrate of the Daresbury'Division, will move that application be made to the Secretary of State for a copy of the public general statutes, to be allotted to the Daresbnry Divisionior the use of the Cona. The Deputy Clerk of the Peace will lay before the Court a letter fr,,m the Clerk of the Runcorn Union, on the subject of a revision of the basis of the county rates. The Court will meet by adjourn- went at Knutsford on Wednesday, the 29th inst.

I TEE SOTJTEPORT BANE, —At the adjourned meeting of the Southport Town Council, on Friday evening, the question was raised as to what money the Corporation badl lying at the Southport and West Lancashire Bank.—Coun- cillor Gregory remarked that he found that the Corporation were debtors to banks to the amount of t£15,318. He wanted to know what the difference of interest was, and what they were paying to those various banks in the way of interest; and within what period an end would be put to these matters. It was very inconvenient, very expensive, and a great lcem to Southport. —Alderman Fisher, as chairman of the Finance Committee, referring tothe Southport and West Lancashire Bank and the account of the Corporation there- with, observed drat he could say that there were three things which the reconstruction committee had to do. One was to get the old shares transferred, the second to get the preference shares taken up, and the third to get the share- holders' sanction to re-open the bank. The first two things had been done, but the third was yet to be done. As soon as the bank doors were opened the money owing to the Cor- poration would be paid forthwith, and provision was being made for that object. When the day arrived for opening the doors of the bank—and they would be opened before the I first week in July—the payment of the money would be taken in hand. The interest which was Wog charged on that account wde a matter entirely in the hands of the liqui- dators of the bank. Since the Slat of March the Corpora- tion had borrowed £13,065, and they had paid off £10,065. The money in the West Lancashire Bank (about £23.000) was not the fault of the borough treasurer, but (Mr. Fisher remarked) was entirely the fault of the members of the Cor- poration itselL—During the discussion many acrimonious words were used, many of the members hoping that when the bank was opened such a state of things would not be allowed to occur again.

THE Cos Ix SOUTH-WEST LANCASTHEE.—An Ormakirk correspondent writes :—The thunderstorm of the past few days have done no damage of any moment to the crops. The genial rains have etfected a fwonderful change in the ap- pearance of the crops, and both corn and grass hive been greatly benefitted. There is good grazing for stock, and the meadows show rapid improve- ment. The, grass crop in some districts will be much heavier than was anticipated. Cutting has com- menced between Liverpool and Ormskirk with very satisfac- tory results, clover especially being good. It is anticipated that wheat will make an excellent crop, the moisture being of great service. In many districts it is already" shooting," —fully a week or two earlier than of late years • while in thq neighbourhood of Liverpool may be seen fiekls in full ear—an exceptional circumstance considering the season passed through. Potatoes look remarkably well. Oats pro- mise fairly. Of the orchard crops it may be remarked that they will be about an average. A scheme is on feot for the drainage oC the low-lying meadows between Liverpool and Preslon, chiefly owned by the Earl of Sefton and the Mar- quis de Casteja, thousands of acres of which are flooded annually, causing immense losses to the farmers in this im- portant agricultural division. Martin Mere, a wide expanse of country, is likewise to be drained, the landowners (inclu- ding Lord Derby, Sir T. G. Fermor-Ilesketh, the Scarisbrick Trustees, die.) having united in the matter. This is a con- summation which has been aimed at for years. When it is carried out there can be no doubt that the benefit to be derived from the two schemes by the farmers of South Lan- cashire will be incalculable.

SUNDAY &moor. FESTIVAL AT Parrzzyn.—The annual festival in connection with the Penketh Wesleyan Sunday School passed off with considerable eclat yesterday. The day was most auspicious for such an event, the sky being unclouded, and the sun's rays,ternpered by a pleasant breeze, dissipatei all thoughts of weariness. The scholars number- ing 250 were formed into processional order in the school- room at one o'clock, thence proceeding to Vine House, the residence of Mrs. Garpett. Dressed- in their best the children presented a very pretty appearance, and, with the numerous banners which they carried, made the quiet lanes through which they passed appear quite festive. From Vine House the procession proceeded to Miss Gandy's, Sunnvside, Mr. Dutton's, Penketh Lodge, the house of Mrs. Rontledge, an old teacher, who is at prement ill; on to Mr. Robert Garnett', Hall Nook ; and Brookside, the residence of Mr. David Garnett. At each place the scholars sang a hymn and received nuts and gingerbread. Mar R. Garnett presented each scholar with a small book. On arriving at Brookside, the scholars were regaled with a capital tea, on the grass facing the house, the novelty of the situation adding much to its enjoyment by the children. Afterwards an adjournment was made to the recreation 'ground, where various games were indulged ha until dusk, when a meeting was held at the schoolroom, for the purpose of distributing prizes to those scholars who had been most regular in their attendance at school during the year. A number of special r:zes were also given by Mrs. R. Garnett. Much credit is due to Messrs. J. Watson (superintendent), Hobson, Mainly, and Atherton for the completeness of the arrangements. To-day (Saturday) the teachers will have annual pic-nie, the place chosen for the day's outing being the old city of Chester.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

Now that there is no big sensation on hand and the newspaper columns are frequently dull to dreariness the smallpox scare monopolises a large share of public attention in the metropolis and other large towns. I hear that several of the younger members of the House of -Commons have been vaccinated "off hand," that ladies rush pell mell into railway smoking compartments in order to cultivate the fumes of the once noxious weed as a disinfectant, and that °there of the fair sex are busy upon a variety of in- genious expedients for protecting their arms while in a state of "vaccine sensitiveness," many ladies using slings, while two or three have been seen in the park with their arms in showy ivory frameworks. Who can help admiring the , persistency and ingenuity of woman. Even out of a small- pox scare she will obtain something that shall be, "the rage:" The Shopwoman's grievance is again coming to the front. In spite of the protests of the Press, in spite of the prompt- ings of common sense, and in spite of the wishes of the majority of their customers tradesmen still persist in the ! stupid and senseless practice of compelling their female assistants tastand behind thecounter all day. The injurious and painful task of standing behind a counter for eight, nine, or ten hours at a stretch imposed upon delicate girls must imperceptibly, but surely, undermine their constitu- tions, and parents who send their daughters to establish- ments where this kind of thing is practised are as much to blame as the managers. The evils of the present system have been repeatedly pointed out by medical men. [appeal to any man, blinded though he may have been to the fact hitherto by the film of custom, whether it is possible for a girl after spending years of enervating toil in this way to grow into a healthy woman. Anyone with the slightest knowledge of the formation of the human body will l,now it is impossible. And when a few seats behind the counter make all the difference—convert a wretched girl into a happy I one, make the smile on her face when serving a customer real instead of assumed, and giving her the opportunity of growing into a heathy woman instead of a whining hypochondriac—l am amazed that so much entreaty and persuasion are required to Induce tradesmen to break away from old customs and to treat their female assistants as though they were human beings. Dr. A. W. Edis, whn, as physician to the Dressmakers' Institution. has had excep- tioeal opportunities of knowing the reality and extent of the injury resulting to health from the present absurd cus- tom, says that varicose veins, severe indigestion, nervous prostration, back-ache, bead-ache, loss of appetite and general debility are, in the majority of instances, the in- evitable result of their incessant standing from morning till night. The latest ness from America is that the Legisla- ture of New York have without a dissentient voice passed a bill compelling shopkeepers to furnish seats behind the counters for their employes. I should be glad to see a similar bill passed in this country. but I see no hope for this during the present year. It is, however, satisfactory to learn that some of the leading shopkeepers in London have set an example which I hope will be followed by the trades- men of this and all other towns in the kingdom.

Perhaps with a laudable desire to see Rome, the Rev. Canon Barclay, M. A., of Runcorn, has gone upon the con- tinent, but the reverend gentleman's absence from home is likely to be sadly felt at the Parish Church if one is to judge from what took place there on Sunday evening. The arrangements for supplying the pulpit with a true successor of the apostles seem to have been perfect as far as the morning's service was concerned, when a stranger preached on behalf of the society for propagating the gospel amongst the scattered children of Abraham. However, when the evening service should have commenced, it was found that there was no clergyman, and the "fleck," was without a shepherd. Mr. Edward Imison went to the reading desk, and gave out a hymn, probably thinking that by the time the singiftg had ceased, the reverend gentleman who was expected would make his appearance. But "the unexpected always happens," according to. the late Lord Beaconsfield, and the minister did not arrive. Mr. Johnson, the organist, played another voluntary. He might very well have given "All we like sheep, from the famous oratorio. Then one of the choir, a Mr. Joule, was deputed to run up to Newtown and fetch the Rev. J. J. Bryant, who I was preaching there. Whilst he was on his journey a certain I gentleman, who is not credited with the most delicate taste, walked down the principal aisle with a very dignified carriage, and left the building. At about seven o'clock, Mr. Bryinit arrived and went through the service. I do not know , who is really to blame for this state of matters, but one would thick that if it be the Vicar his comfort would not have been increased if it had been possible to let him know the condition of his dock on this particular evening. %S healer under the magnificent dome of St. Peter's, or that of the Church of Notre Dame, he would most probably have wished himself back in quiet Runcorn, so that he could have Seoll to matters being conducted to his satisfaction in FLACCUS. the sanctuary.

A meeting of Scotch members of Parliament was held yesterday afternoon in one of the conference rooms at the House of Commons, for considering the state of Scotch business in Parliament and ascertaining the views of mem- hers as to what measures should have the preference this session. There were about forty Scotch members present and among those who took part were Sir W. Harcourt, Mr ' Mundella, the Lord Advocate, and the Solicitor General for Scotland. An informal discussion took place lasting about two hours, the result showing that the bill most in favour was the Educational Endowments Bill for Scotland. The bill next in favour appeared to he the Entail Bill, the object of which it was stated was to assimilate the Scotch 'as much as possible to the English law in that respect. It ; was understood that the Poor Law Bill and the Sheriff Sales Bill might be allowed to stand over, with several other measures, until neat session, whilst the passage of the bills generally approved by the conference would be pressed this session.

Lord Salisbury, speaking yesterday, at Willis's Rooms, London. at a meeting for the promotion ef the higher educa- tion of women at King's College, said the highest object of instruction was not merely to cram the mind with facts, but to produce a taste for intellectual pursuits, and by the reforming influence of reading and of thought to oust thoeo base comp, titiona for the human affections. The education of women as a practical question had passed the stage of argument, and now the question was in whose hands should that education fall. Lord Carnaryon recommended the King's College scheme.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

Fgra AT OVER HALL.—By the kind permission Of Capt. Turner, J.P., of Over Hall, a benefit fête and bazaar for the Darnhall school was held on Friday and Saturday on his grounds. Though the first day was anything but agreeable as to weather, yet there were many of the gentry and trades- men of the town present. The attraction of the grounds, the neat and varied style (Italian) in which they are laid out, the extent of the westerly view, and last, not least, the interest of so many fair ones in a generous project will sufficiently account for quality snaking up for quantity. The bind, under their able leader Mr. S. Hulse, played selec- tions of music at intervals, which sot those light of toe if not of heart "to thread the mazy dance." Thus the delapi- dated schools, the attractive grounds, and the winsome ladies, all contributed their quota in bringing a goodly num- ber to the fête, especially on the second day. The most fruitful way to raise the fun Is was raffling. Everything of value was raffled for, and so it happened one won a cheese, I another an umbrella a third a screen, a painting or a fish, I de. The day's proceedings were varied by athletic sports. the following being the prize winners :-120 yards: let, 1 405., N. G. Woodyatt ; 2nd, 15s, G. Radcliffe: and 3rd, 5s I J. Ball. 440 yards :-Ist, 30s, H. Penketh ; 2nd, 10s, H. I Barlow; 3rd, ss, A. Cooke. 220 yards handicap :-Ist, silver teapot (gift of Captain Turner). N. G. Woodyatt ; 2nd, 10s, T. B. Atherton; 3rd, ss, S. Clough. 1760 yards ;—let, 40s, S. Hunt: 2nd, 15s, G. Rowland; 3rd. ss, J. Stubbs. 440 yards hurdle race :—lst, 255, H. Penketh ; 2ad, 15s, N. G. Woodyatt ; 3rd, 55., G. Rowland. Another source of attrac- tion as such is always at Winsford, was the christy's min- strels. It made little difference their being amateurs. The troupe did their part worthily, and they had their reward. Thus the useful, comic, and physical contributed some- thing; but the best part in Oh whole affair was the com- missariat department, presided over by the hostess and various ladies in a most efficient manner. The amount raised was handsome. WINSFORD IMPROVEMENTS.—This town seems to be con- tinually in a state of improvement. House building on the most approved principles, road mending with special refer- ence to economy, street or rather causeway paying with a sufficiency of time for consolidation between one part and another. Now the bridge is being lifted some five feet up above what it has been for a while back; the result of which is that everyone must move their tenements upward, or else appear to sink below a habitable position. The fact is, if this continual raising process could be kept on, Winsford Hill would disappear, Gravel Hill would be no more, and the market-place would be level with the general tableland that stretches between Winsford and Middlewich.

• THE NEW ARMY ORGANISATION SCHEI4E.-0/1 the motion for going into Supply on the army estimates, Mr. CRILDERS brought forward the consideration of the new army organisa- tion scheme, and explained various portions of it. It had only been after most careful consideration that it had been decided not to re-engage private soldiers after their 12 years service if they had not at the end of that term earned their stiipes and become corporals. He believed the new scheme would improve the character of the army, improving as it would the pay of both officers and men, and secure for both a good prospect of a steady flow of promotion. He defended the change as regards the terri- torial regiments, and the general result of the scheme would be to improve the stamp of the men entering the army and to diminish desertisn.—Sir W. BARTELLOT contended that the proper time for enlistment was ten years, and said the Transvaal showed the result of "lending out young soldiers. —Sir A.
