THE AGITATION IN IRELAND.

Intelligence reached Dublin, on Monday, of an attempted assassination in the county Galway. One account says As Mr. Lambert, of Aggard, was to-day proceeding to the residence of his son, near Gort, he was fired at from behind a hedge and severely wounded; but it is thought there is no immediate danger of his life. The would-he assassin fired four shots. The occurrence was immediately made known to the constabulary of Craughwell, who proceeded to the scene of the outrage. No arrests have yet been made. Mr. Lambert's son, who travelled with his father', was also wounded. Another account says that as Mr. Lambert and his son were proceeding along the road at 25 minutes to 12 o'ci..ek. three shots were fired at them in quick succession from tehinl a ditch; happily the two gentlemen escaped uninjured. Two men, named Moriarty and Shea, were charged at Tralee Petty Sessions, on Monday, with attacking the house of a farmer named Looney, at night, and demanding arms. Three constables who were on patrol duty heard a noise in the neighbourhood of Loonev's house, and on going there they found the house surrounded by men, who were di- zuised. They arrested the prisoners after a severe struggle. Moriarty had his face blackened, and he wore a sack over his clothes. The prisoners were returned for trial, bail being refused. Mr. Sexton, M.P., complained at Tuesday's meeting of the Land League, that funds were not lowing in so freely as formerly, The receipts last week amounted to only £970, and of this .£BOO was from the Irish World. The time, he said, had arrived when it was necessary for their friends in all parts of the world to cast their resources on the side of the League. Three Roman Catholic priests have sailed from Queenstown for New York, on a lecturing tour through the,Dnited States. One of them casries with him a letter from Archbishop Croke, commissioning him to "proclaim everywhere an America what the Irish people want and what they do not want." It is reported that Mr. Parnell has decided to go to America, after "seeing the Land Bill through Committee," and enter upon an extended political tour. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, it is added, will probably accompany his chief.

div.head: RACE FRIDAY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: RACE FRIDAY AT ST. HELENS.

On this day (Friday) it is usual for the various Snnday Schools in the town to have their field days, which operate as a counter attraction to the proceedings at Newton. It is also usual for some of the tradesmen to close their. shops, and the appearance of the town indicates that the day is set apart by general enjoyment.' The Congregational Sunday School have arranged for a trip to Llandudno. The scholays of the Parish Church Schools will march from the schools at half past twelve, headed by Messrs. Webster's and End] es's brass band, to Mrs. Littlei's field, Derton's Green. The Wesleyan Sunday scholars will proceed to Rainhill asylum, and walk through the gardens, as on former occasions. The Primitive Metholists, Kirkland-street, whose scholars num- bar about 330, will assemble at the school at half past twelve and walk to Moss Bank where they will enjoy themselves in a field lent for the occasion by Mr. Richard Fishwick. Tea will be provided for the scholars on the field, weather per- mitting at five *lock, and parents and teachers will be able to obtain refreshments in the barn. The scholars of the Nutgrove Wesieyans are going to a field at 'Matto Heath, lent by Mr. Naylor as in previous years, and the scholars of the Park-road Baptists in a field at Gerard's Bridge, lent by Mr. Jacques. The Park-read Primitive Methodists will visit ,the grounds of Mr. Brimeloyr at Garwood, and the scholars of Windle Schools will find amusement at Hare's Finch, in a field belonging to Mr. I've. The Rwenhead and Parr AI onnt Church scholars will join together in a field at Thatto Heath. The United Methodist and Presbyterian Schools are withholding their treats for a future occasion. This morning (Friday) about 400 people booked to Llandudno. on the Congregational trip, but this number would be augmented at Peasley Cross, and the stations be- tween that place And Widnes. About 60 persons connected with the Church of Christ, Bickerstaffe-street, went by train to Frodsham, where they will enjoy themselves the greater part of the day. The streets of the town appear very animated, but the shops are not all closed. This afternoon the Holy !Trinity Church, Parr Adonnt, are gobs; from Peasley Cross to Sutton Oak by rail.- The shortness of the distance has been the subject of much amasement and plea- sant chaff. A considerable number have gone by road and rail to Newton.

A fine young shark. 8 feet 3 inches in length, and measur- ing 3 feet 11 [riches in girth, was captured in the inner harbour at Torquay on Thesdar'evening. A child named Rebecca Jackson, aged four years, was found dead on Monday evening at her parent's house in Liverpool by a clergyman, who called there in the course of his isinistrations. A doctor, who was sent for. expressed his belief that death had been caused by strangu- lation; and it is ifuspected that the. mother, the wife of a sailor and a woman of very respectable character, merdered the child in a fit of insanity. When taken int 6 custody, she declared she" did it to save its multi." Mrs. Jackson is not yet in a fit condition to be brought before the magistrates. Mr. illundella, writing to one of his constituents, says be believes that when the Land Bill is passed Irishmen will appreciate the honest desire of the Government to do jnstice to the Irish tenant and make Inqand prosperous and con- tented. Nothing has been more painful in his political experience than the cruel necessity imposed upon the G..- 'ferment of asking Parliament for additional powers to suppress violence and maintain the law, pertdingthe enact. meat of remedial measures. It seemed unjust that the' Liberal party should, be reaping the fruits ofl neglect ter which they were not responaible. COLLECTING THE TICICETE.—A rood story was told apropos of a Roble lord who was recently returning from the races. In the adjoining compartment were, eight book- makers who, cleaned out by successive failures,. Irate travelling without tickets, hotting by a turn of good luck to escape payment. At last one of them during a stoppage hit upon a brilliant idea.,. P.ulling his cap, down over' iris- eyes and La Atoning his coat he went to the •carriage of, the noble lord and his frieuda; and, assuming an official air, col- tented all their tickets. These. he distributed. among his own friends,and ow the train reachingbLonden the noble lord had a narrow escape of seeing himself and his friends taken into milady for attempting to defraud the railway company, for despite their assurances the officials declined to believe that anyone had been audacious enougb tee collet the passengers' tickets. Ample preparation lead been made for the recep- tion of the delegates and visitors who were lodged at the houses of the various members a the congregation. Each day dinnee and tea was served in the school-room, and every- thing passed off pleasantly. The' proceedings really corn- nienced on Saturday evening;when a hand meeting was held irithe Friers' Green Chapel, and on Sunday services were held in Friars' Green Chapel, preached by Messrs. Thoinis, Jackson (Burnley), W. Sanderson -(Liverpool), and Win.' Oxley (Manchester) ; Stockton Heath, W. Bradshaw (Neld son); Buckley•street Chapel, A. Roscoe (M igan), and W. Branfoot (Sunderland); Workingmen's Mission, Bank Qriay, S. Cooke (Sindsley).; and M. Kennedy (Wigan) ; Academy-street Chapel; W. Brimelow (Button), and W. San. derson ; Lawton Common, B. Dyson (Oldham); Culcheth,' W. H. Ward (Liverpool) ; Present, Joseph Settle (Bolton). A detailed' account of the proceedings will be found below. PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS. ' .„ MO Las. yT; in addressing the meeting, said : . I TM-VW i • nkful to God that I am permitted to meet yen °nee, i ire, and especially in Warrington. I am re- mindedettlii niftily happy seasons I have enjoyed in con- nection with'The,Warfington Church. -More than 40 years are passed away sirce I first had the privilege of visiting brethren in this town. Most if not all the honoured men who then ministered the "Word of Life" have gone to their reward. And although transplanted in the skies, praise God, younger in their stead continue to arise. I can- not but contrast the state of our churches when I first I visited the friends here with their present condition. We are too apt to draw unfavourable inferences from the paucity of. our members when compared with other Christian organisations around us. I should rejoice were our numbers i a thousand times as many more than they are. But lam by no means discouraged with the position we at present hold. Our path, from the first, has been very difficult, arising from a variety of causes. the chief cause being the anaount of self sacrifice required of those who labour in word and doctrine. To be a free gospel minister is no sine- cure, (Ilear,,bear.) He is to be an example of industry, diligent in business, to "work and eat his own bread,— (hear, bear)—and be has to give attendance to reading." To do so books Will have to be purchased. He has the Gospel to preach, often far away from home, and the Church te feed and: oversee, added to whie.h:the temporal circumstances of our brethren are, as a rule, very limited. Notwithstand- ing these disadvantages we have great cause to praise God that He has continued to raise up and qualify men amongst us who cheerfully and zealously give themselves to the blessed work. Forty years ago there were not 20 churches in our union, and several of them but imperfectly organieed. We had about ten chapels, most of them wanting in corn- 'fort inside and attraction outride. Nor was the schoolmaster abroad. Most of our members and office bearers were in- debted to the Sunday school for what little learning they possessed. We had no hymn book and had to pay large prices to those who very unwillingly.sold them to us. We had to contend with the opposition of the influential de- nominations who thought our free principles would sub- vert the Christian ministry, and injure the church of Christ. The greatest obstacle in the way of our progress was that public opinion was against us. Our principles, especially a free church and a free ministry, were looked upon as vision- ary and Utopian; while the honoured and disinterested men who were engaged in propagating them were branded as dis- affected, penurious, and troublers of God's Israel. We had to contend not only with opposition from the ungodly and the enemies of .the truth, but from these who professed faith in the Lord Jesus, which was the more diStressing coming from members of the church of God. These were some of the hindrances our fathers had to contend against. The wonder is that they were not discouraged. But they had counted the coat and bad faith in God and in the truth they had expensed. They were ready to admit that their free prin- ciples were in advance; of the times in which they lived, but of their ultimate triumph they had no doubt... All honour to them who" ont of weakness were made strong, and waxed valiant in fight," and handed down to us the pure and dis- interested principles of the New Testament. Thank God the divine leaven of freedom has been silently and effectively working, and the proof is before us. (Hear,hear.) Our minutes of last year furnish the following interesting; information :-- Eighty five chapels. most of them commodious, well siteated and comfortable; 4,584 members; 257 ministers; 93 schools; 1,681 teachers; 13.495 scholars, making a total at near 20,000 persons, with 20,000 hearers at tenet, who regularly attend our places of worship. There are now facilities for acquir- ing knowledge, which did not exist forty years ago. If our young men avail themselves of the means at hand and give themselves to reading and study, they will become ac- quainted with God, His holy word, His works in nature, with man, his state and his responsibilities, and especially with Jesus and His glorious work of redemption. They will most , assuredly become "workmen that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth." The great change " which has taken place in public opinion in reference to our distinctive principles is indeed encouraging. (Hear, hear.) We now hear from every section of the Christian Church, the cry for what they call lay agency, or voluntary and un- paid labourers. (Hear, hear.) Nor is this change confined to an unpaid ministry,,,Our views on the right of the church to govern is ,extending. Who would have thought a few, years ago 'that the Wesleyan conference would be a represen- tative body? .Thib change in public opinion has changed the law of our land.. The established church cannot now levy church rates. or does she possess the exclusive right to celebrate marriages, and to inter the dead in the church- yards of our country. (Applause.) Can we not trace this expansion of the public mind to the increased knowledge of the Holy scriptures by means of our Sunday schools, and the holy, useful, and sacrificing lives of our predecessors, in the cause of Christ. (Hear' hear.) Looking on the past and viewing the present, we have abundant cause to thank God and take courage. (Hear, hear.) Let us ministers and members give ourselves to God and His cause ; preach and live Christ, and our influence for good will be felt and seen, and a glorious future is in store for our United Free Gospel Churches. (Applause.) We are engaged in a blessed work. It may appear difficult, and our, meani may be limited, but we have the promise of our Divine Master to help, guide, and defend, He is our Lord, our life, and our exceeding great reward. Union with him will not only make failure impos- sible, but give us the full assurance of certain victory. The time is fast approaching when onr scriptural principles asset forth in our testimony will perv:ule the land, and bless our country with the simple and unadulterated truth as it is in Jesus. ,-, My prayer is that we may stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ' hath made lIS free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage. The great reckon- ing day will speedily be ;men us. Each annual meeting records the solemn fact of some of our companions in labour being called to their reward. And what a reward! Not indeeCgold that perisheth, nor the empty honours of this world. but 'glory, and honour, and immortality, )ternal life. Dear brethren we nerve a good master. His work is hononr- glorious, pmducing the greatest luxury that this " feed the flock of God, the oversight thered, not by aeahrlteha can afford: Bo pocourami ; . iYll74tl4erk;i taking not by filthy lucre, but of a ready constraintwhich I mind ;,neither as being lords over God's neritage, but being among btitw enamples to the -flock:- • 'And when the Chief Shepherd shall appear; Ye ehall''reeelye a crown of glory that fadeth not . away." (Applause.) The best thanks of the meeting -were tendered to the presi- dent for his address. ern-the motion of Mr. A. Roscoe. materrott or rtilisMtwe AND VICV-PRESIDEIQI'. The votes were taken by ballot arid after several tsllotings the nominations were rethiced to Messrs. Oxley and Sanderson. The secretary I(Mr. Roscoe), ruled the president to be out of order and the allot was proceeded with, the numbers being declared : i *ley, 35. Sanderson, 33. Mr. 'Oxley then took the chair mid hearty applauss. and returned thtriillts to the meeting ir, r`that mark of their confidence; 'For the office of vice- ' reAdent there were nominated Messrs. M. Kennedy, W. 4anderson, and J. Hudlass. The result of the first ballot . vas Kennedy, 23; Sanderson, 27; and Hudlass, 13. The The latter name was then struck out and another ballot ' aken when Mr. Kennedy received 40, and Mr. Sander- son 29 votes. Mr. -Kennedy was therefore declared 'eteeted E i Mr. ATTOTPITifIRT OF SECRETARIES. M 10. CO* RA& appointed secretary, and Mr. A. Roscoe, Vice secretary. • -

NEW CHURCHES._ Application for admission into the Union from the follow- ing churches had been received and considered by the Con- nexional Committee, and recommended for admittance : Bethany (Sunderland), 103 members; Spring View (Lower Ice), 18 members; Newtown (Pemberton), 31 Members; and Thombull (Ifeed), 30 members. Statements having been made showing the sound-condition these places were at present in, and the excellent prospect before them,-they were unani-. motley admitted into full union, and the representatives, who were warmly welcomed, took their seats. Attercliffe and Denton desired to remain on trial for another year and their

request was granted. , STATE OF THE CHURCHES. The Vice-Secretary (Mr. Roscoe) then read the reports which bad been received from the various churches. On the whole the • reports were very encouraging, and showed the society to be in a flourishing condition, many places being actively engaged in mission work. I An adjournment was then made for dinner which had been provided in the schoolroom for the delegates and those r' 'Biters who ‘had come -from a distance. t . ,' I -1J , - 'ME 'DEATH LIST. 10traniesneningrINM ,- Firth, .of Oldham' in answer to the questifin 't-Have any'cif our ministers died during the year," 'aid Mr. John Meetly, of Oldham district had been'taken itedY,,and his less was much lamented, his connection with I the cirouit having been long and honourable.. , His nanatal tied been first on the plan of preachers for a great number' of Years. The delegates from Leigh reported the death of Mr. Idoseph Hilt, of that place. A resolution, moved by Mr, Sanderson; and seconded by Mr. Roscoe, condoling with the connexion and the churches to which the departed ministers bad belonged, was passed unanimously. ' , THE WORK OF THE CONNEXION. , The Connexional Committee in their report, read by Mr; Roscoe said the matter of the chapel at Cliviger caused much a'nxietv and' labour during the early part of the year, 4tit was finally satisfactorily arranged. The thanks of the *mmittee 'were due to Bro. Jackson, of Burnley,. for the Orery able and timely help he rendered in the affair. Fair r•clak trustees had repertmi being In difficaltiesin money matters and the committee decided to appeal , to ,the ,Conr nexion on their behalf. Bro. Oxley was requested to do for Fair Oak what he had done for Copley Bent—take charge of r the appeal and carry it as far as possible to a successful issue. The sum theehurch wanted was £25, and £2O had been collected and handed over to them with £5 as a loan from the funds. Deputations had waited upon most of the dis- trict er circuit meetings during the year to endeavour to in-1 terest them in the raising of money for mission contingen=, cies and other phrposes. Circulars had been sent out asking for information as to whether there were bands of hope ot other temperance societies in connection with the . various churches and wheels, but not more than 25 replies had been, received. With the exception of about two places, all these churches bad a temperance organisation. The committee' recommended that Newbiggendistrictbe left off the minutes. The committee also nominated four ministers from which to, select two representatives to the approaching Methodist, Ecumenical Council. Mr. Roscoe -stated the numbers of members were this year 4,743, last year 4,584, an increase of 159. But they had that morning taken into conneAion our.churchea with 199 members, so that there was really,* decrease of 40 members in the churches represented at th ae; st annual meeting.--The report of the Evangelistic Com- mittee which consisted of 'Messrs. Boote, Tviiss, Brimelew,, Kennedy, Wild, Oxley, and Hudlass, stated that Bro. Lee had been appointed to the Wigan circuit, that-being a large and increasing district ; and Bro. Berry's operations had not been confined to any place for more than three weeks at a time. • £2OO had been lent to the brethren at Cliviger, near BUrnley, and there was now a flourishing church in that tillage. There was an excellent mission-room in Channett- street, Manchester, and divine worship was cenducted there every Sabbath. At a meeting of the committee, held on the Bth March, the treasurer stated that the income up to date stmounted to £169, expenditure, £230. Mission-rooms had been opened in Trafford-road, Manchester, and in Eccles, and the cause was prospering. Mr. R. CUNLIFFE read the report of the Book-room Com- mittee, which urged upon the meeting the importance of increasing the circulation of the magazine, and stated that permission had been received for it to be placed on the table of the Young Men's Christian Association, London, in addi- tion to that at Manchester. It was also received by the Great and Little Bolton free libraries, through the efforts of the churches there, and the committee recommended the other churches to make similar efforts. A complaint was made at the last annual meeting that there were no tracts specially advocating their principles. Since that time several thousands had been printed. The committee had on hand forrnulants for the solemnisation of matrimony and the burial of the dead, prepared by Mr. Sanderson. The hymn book still maintained its position, the number sold during the year being 2,592. The total number sold up to the present time was 29,647. The committee appointed to prepare a tune book had considered a large number of tunem and adopted about 600, some from standard authors ands some original, a tune having been selected from each meter in their hymn book. This would be a boon to the churches, - and meet a long felt want. The book would be placed in the hands of members at the earliest possible time. 1 i A discussion, introduced by Mr. Firth, followed the read- ing of these reports on the importance of evangelical work, Ind the way it should be conducted, to secure the most beneficial results, it being suggested by several delegates that frequent visits should be paid to those churches which were in low condition.—The VICE-CHAIRMAN remarked that as the Connexion had only three missionariee their opera. done must be somewhat limited, and pointed out that the income for the work only amounted to about £3OO, whereas if each member would contribute id. per week, an income of £l,OOO would be realised. If that were done the work would receive an impetus and be much extended. On the motion of Mr. SECKER (Thornhill Edge), seconded by Mr. JOHN PARR (Bolton), the reports were unanimously adopted. Mr. SANDERSON offered up prayer, and the Conference adjourned.

their departure as best they ynight. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him, the more he thought el- 44 that tbese "distinctions, which they found were extensively recognised—the dis- tinctions between the clergy and the laity—were a very serious element of weakness in the moral and spiritual power of the Church of Christ. In this way—it introduced two _ _ _ _ _

- different standards of religious life. fhey found a common expectation conning all through society that the clergyman was -Tented to live a purer and a holier life than their Coil rt layman, who had 'to do with the business of the wort.; He knew nothing more injurious; nothing more con- trary to the glorious spirit of the gospel, which would get hold of every man, whether he be clergyman or layman, and lift hint up to the highest exaltation of goodness. (Heat, hear.) They heard a good deal said from time to time about, the disinclination of the masses to have anything to do with religion, and it did strike - one as an astonishing thing that with all the agencies they had, so little progress was being made. Mr. Murrell had btirne his testimony—and he was a Man, who, by his lectures at Man- Chester, and more recently at London and other parts of the country, had.come in contact with the masses as much as anyone, and be said one of the great reasons why working- . inen would have nothing to do with the churches, was this broad gulf which separates the clergyman from the laity. He said it was one of his primary objects to tklealr 'down the barrier, andto do away with all these distinctions that exist between the clergy and the laity. He had followed! the example of Mr. Dale and Mr. Spurgeon, by himself abolishing everything that shaped of distinction between the minister and the people—the clergy and the laity. (Applause.) He (the speaker) thought that the promotion of the cause of God by the preaching of the Gospel upon pure and disinterested principles, would raise that Gospel in • the minds and hearts of the people, and would raiser and elevate those whmwere engaged in preaching it. (Applause:) Mr. M..K.Earangtav said some time ago a distinguished man, a man who had created a :great deal-of eteitement in the country, delivered a denture, rand his subject was, "What has Christianity done for the working classes?" In the course of the lecture he tried to prove that Chrisianity svas a failnre, that it was the working man's enemy. He (the speaker) thought it was a mistake, and would start from the same point. What has Christianity &me for the work- ing classes? In the first place, it was necessary thershould know what Christianity was. The lecturer started wrong— his premises were wrong, and consequently his conclusion wereerroneous. instead of saying what Christianity was he talked a good deal about the 39 Articles. He did not know that they had anything to do with those. (Laughter.) They had only three( hear, hear)—faith, hope, and charity. Love to God and love' to man was the great distinguishing princigle of Christianity. (Hear, hear.) Love worketh no ill torbis neighbour. Who was their neighbour ? _Every- body. (Hear, hear.) Then if love worked no ill to his neighbour, all the ills that afflict society come from some other source. (Hee, hear.) People thought Christianity should do what it did not propose to do. It did not propose to make idle men happy. He who would not work ought not to eat. Some of them did. (Laughter.) But men who consumed more than they produced were enemies of society. It did not propose to make a sensuous man happy. What did it propose to do ? It propesed. in the first place, to giver a man power over him- self, and he (lid not think they need try to conquer others until they bad managed themaelves. It proposed to make a man amoral hero, to give him sufficient stamina and spiritual power to enable bins to conquer him- self, to prevent him following the lust of the flesh. It pro- ' posed to make a man happy and keep Him happy.- It pro- posed also to cum all the moral evils under the sun, and its precepts when they were received and reduced to practise were certain to accomplish all that it proposed to do. But it did not propose to remove all these evils unless its condi- tions were complied with. The moral condition of the people when Christianity commenced operations was some- thing fearful. It seemed to have got to it lowest point. What did Christianity do then ? In 80 years Christianity had produced an entire revolution. They gave Rochdale credit for starting co-operative principles. Why the apostles started them on a broader basis. They had one common fund. What had Christianity done for the workingmen ? It started with the workingmen, and in a short time Chris- tianity had done more for the workingm n than all the systems of the philosophers ever attempted. From the beginning of Christianity down through the 18 centuries it had been the friend of the working classes, What hid it done for society generally? Christianity began in trying to break down the barriers that existed between man and map, (Hear, hear.) It was the first system in the world that preached up the brotherhood, and they need not confine thercetelvewto Christian literature as they could find evi- dence.ontside, Working men were indebted for every civil and religious liberty more to Christianity than to any other system or all systems put together. (Applause.) Mr. SANDERSON, in the course of his remarks, said be had found that there was that scattereth and yet increaseth, and just in proportion as he had given to the cause of God. He had returned it in some cases 30 and 60 fold. That was the greatest gathering they had ever had, and he was glad it had taken place at Warrington. Onward was te he their 'motto, but he believed they would not get up to a state of perfec- tion until the pew vied with the pulpit. and then a stream of blessings would visit the earth and men be brought to a saving acquaintance with Christ. (Applause.) Mr. BRANFOOT (Sunderland) gave an interesting account of the history of the Sunderland church and the manner in which they became acquainted with the connexion. The meeting closed with the benediction.
TUESDAY'S CONFERENCE.

THE MODE OF ELECTING PRESIDENT. At the last annual meeting it was resolved that'afteithe' office of President had been held for two years, liislitAld only be re-elected by a Majority Of three-fourths of the meeting. This now came up for confirma- tion, but the largeness of the majority required, met with some oppmsition. Mr. Redmayne moved that it be r made., a, standing order,, hfit ,Mr. Brimelonv, ttiough of opinion that the President after the second year of office should have a larger majority than formerly, thought two-thirds of the .meeting would be ptifficiently large. THE AFGHAN AND TRANSVAAL WAR.

The following resolution moved by Mr. Bnotron'r, was passed :—" That this assembly hereby expresses hearty gratitudeto the Right Hoc. W. E. Gladstone, the Right Hon. John Bright, and their colleagues in the Government,,. for their efforts to restore peace in Afghanistan and South Africa, and trusts that a policy of justice and riglsteousnes towards those parts of the wOrld may assist in preparing the hearts of the people for the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. This Assembly also views with cordial approbation the en:. deavors of the Great Powers of Europe to settle questions of grave international difficulty by peaceful means, and most fervently prays that the time may speedily, come when wars shall cease, and perpetua peace prevail among all nations." —The resolution were ordered to be sent to the Premier and Home Secretary, bearing the signatures of the president and secretary. -

div.head: NEXT MEETING. PLACE.
div.p: THE NEXT MEETING. PLACE.

The delegates front Nelson and Liverpool each invited the connexion to hold its newt meeting at -their places of wor- ship. It transpired that Liverpool had received a visit since Nelson and on the vote being taken, the invitation of the latter Place was accepted. VOTE OF THANKS. Mr. Dvsote proposed that the beet thanks of the meeting be given to their Waerington friends who had so kindly ministered to their comforts. Especially 'would he mentioh the ladies. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The motion was seconded by Mr. Baeleroor, and carried with acclamation. THE REVISED NEW TESTAMENT. Mr. W. Bnimetow read a paper on the Revised New Testament. After defining what was meant by inspiration, he said the original manuscripts of the writings of the apostles and evangelists had long since been lost, but thousands of copies had been made during the first few centuries of the Christian era. The present revisers had been able to give a more -correct translation than was the case some centuries ago, having had at their disposal several earlier manuscrips. When the translation of 1611 was made, the copies of the Scripture dated back to the twelfth century, but since that time manuscripts dating so far back as the fourth and fifth centuries had been dis- covered. In the course of time words changed their mean- ing, and many English words did not convey the same meaning as they did 200 years ago. (Hear; hear.) . Hence the need of the revision. He thought the opinions generally seen in the newspapers as to how the revision had beep performed had been hasty, ill advised— (hear, hear)—and the result of imperfect informa- tion and ill formed judgment. It was to he taken for granted that 20 of the most learned men of the day, and composed of different denominations in compiling the great work, bad produced results which would bear much better criticism and more careful study than newspaper writers seemed to think. Mr. Brimelme cited a large number of passages which had been coneiderably improved, without alteration in their meaning, and noteinfainging upon the vital truths which concern individual principles. The doctrine of the trinity was still sustained in the passage where the disciples were instructed to "baptise all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." They had also Jesus' divinity and creative power, and his pre-existence asserted, The incarnation and the supernatural circumstance of the birth of our Lord was clearly stated, and they also had in language very little dif- ferent in the new book from the old, that priceless and blessed doctrine of the atonement. All the vital truths of the Gospel and all the doctrines of the Christian religion were abundantly sustained and confitmed by the new revision. He claimed that the new revision strengthened their prin- ciples, and quoted several passages to show that the bishops, elder% and pastors of the New Testament—there who had charge of churches—had to maintain ''themeelves, and the modern system of making • a trade of the ministry was wholly contrary to the spirit of the New Testament. (Hear, hear.) The bishops had to maintain themselves and to do their share in supporting- the churches. Therefore they had reason to welcome the new revision as conforming and strengthening the principles on •whiela their denomination was founded. He recommended preachers to become acquainted with the different renderings between the new and the old Testameht, because in rimy cases difficifities were cleared up, and it was desirable that preachers should have all the light they possibly could. He also thought no text should be taken which wee not in the new revision,— and there were many passages struck out—and that no pas- sage should be quoted which was not in the new book, or at least to say it was not in the revised version. lie would not recommend the adoption of the revised version in their churches and schools until• the whole scriptures were out. He had been much gratified with the great im- pulse given to the reading of the New Testament by the work of the revision—(hear, hear)—and he hoped that when the whole of the Bible was before them they woala have such a reading of it that they had net had since that ism(' by James I. (Applause.) Mr. SANDERSON Moved that the best thanks of the meet- ing be given to Mr. Briraelow for his aIA paper. So far 'ache had read the revised version it strengthened their position as the United Free Gospel Church in no small de- gree. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BRANFOOT' seconded the motion, which wet Sup- ported by Mr. Cook and the President, and carried unani- mously. It was then proposed by Mr. COOK and seconded by Mr. SANDERSON, "That this assembly of delegates of Free Gospel Cherches hails with gratitude to God the new version of the New Testament. It recognises with thank- fulnees the manifestation of earnest research its appearance has brought forth; and especially does it rejoice in its affirmation of our distinctive principles." The proposition was carried. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: TEMPERANCE MEETING.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MEETING.

At the temperance meeting held in the evening, there was a moderate attendance, Mr. W. Wright presiding. The CHAIRMAN remarked that he was particularly pleased that their annual gathering had associated itself with a move- ment so important and lying as it did in close, association with all that was good and beneficial to mankind. (Hear, bear.) He trusted that so far as Friars' Green Chapel was concerned, or the church was concerned, or the people were concerned, that they would never cease to hold the proud position that they had held for so many years in the front ranks of the supporters cf 'temperance reform. (Hear, hear. He was reminded before he came to the meeting by ilke3or the old friends, an old worker in the temperance cadofe, that it Was now 47 years since they Opened the doors of the old chapel to the temperanCo- reformers of that inte and, young as he waS, comparatively sPettking, he,knew that in his boyhood he was aware of the fact' that, when the temperance question, was kickel about here atid there the church found a home for its advocacy with very signal success. There might be some present and there might be some outsido who might think the meeting was scarcely in harmony with the other meetings that had taken place in connection with the annual gathering. It was quite true that the other meetings had been purely of a rellgisus and spiritual character, but be neverthelets bd•

perance principles, ;as certainly in harmony with all they. had had, in view in the other, meetings in connection with i their annual assembly. If it be true, as be believed it to be, thst the success of temperance Work 'would result in the' bettering di Oh condition of the people generally and im- proving themAn a civil, domestic, and moral sense—if it would tend &their improvement morally and physically as _ _ _ . . . . .

be believ'ed it-would,— then he considered that'iti a meeting such as that, with those expectations and hopes, they were indeed helping forward the cause of religion ana the Gospel It mattered not in what part of the town they lived, they had daily under their observation the evils of •tholdrieking habits and .customii of society which told.,them that the drink was bad, that there was 130 good in connection with it, and that it must necessarily result in the ruin and destruction of those who tampered with it. That being so he did not think he needed a single .further argument to induce all good people to put their hands tci this work, And help to save their, fellows from evil and from destruction—Morally, physically, _ _ .

intellectually, and aocially; He was satisfied, "and had been satisfied a very long time, that all who professed to be fol- lowers of Christ, all who professed to make the Gospel the rule Of their lives should certainly have nothing to do with drink. Professing ,Christians should be determined to be 'clear of this great scourge, this great evil which was doing to, much damage in their midst. ' They might advance the Cause of temperance in two erthree ways. ,They might help Op temperance by personal abstinence, and that was perhaps tle most important matter that they should take iuto their , 'consideration in relation to this movement. (Hear, hear.) It !wits a source of regret to him that so many who professed' repgion felt free to touch the drink, and to use it as they said, in moderation. That , was a great calamity. It was in his 'estimation the greatest hindrance" in the way of the progress and success of this movement. Ifl the religictus portion of he community would banish 404 ' from their tables and house, he was sure that the prospects of the temperana movement would be greatly improYed for he certainly agreed with what the Right Hon. John, Bright said some years ago. The right hon. gentleman said that for the most part the success of the temperire reform was in the hands of Christian people, and as soo ad Christian people could unite themselves upon this matter they could in a very short time, it, they were disposed to take it up and make it a burning question with them, bring itbefore the public and make it ,one of the leading, nay in- deed the leading question either time, and' wonld Speedily bring about legislation, in reglad torthe matter. Having stated that he and, all the 'members of his family were, teetotallers, he remarked that it they would personally' abstain, and take great care to educate their children, and constantly agitate In OM proper way amongsp4 their fellows to try to inducefthe Governinett to take, by legislative enactments, temptation out of ,the way of their fellows, ,he, felt sure by so doing and using aright their political power they might see the temperance question in a much more prosperous condition 'that it was at the present time and with greater prospects of legislative success. (Applause,) , ,Mr, E. Miss said he would rather persuade a religions man, who was in the habit of ,drinking mederately, to give it up than he would a drunkard to do so, becatise he appre- hended thatrthe restilts would be more blessed in the former', than the latter case. There .was hardly' a man in ten *emend who got enchanted by, these evil abits who could at free from them unless some very powerful or happy In-, was brought to hear upon him, and he was induced' b+ some extraordinami circumstances to become an abstainer. Where drink was Reedit' the greatest moderation the pro- bability was that some members of the family would fall. ancl'eo prevalent were the evils of intetimerence that so far, as his experience went he did not know within the range of his acquaintance end observation a single family that had escaped the evils of intoxicating drinks. When a man rib- stained there was positive safety, and his influence mutst be on the right side. His exantple would tend towards the safety of all with whom be had to do, and he contended that under such circumstances he was doing good by abstain- ing. But if he felt no inclination to support. those on tip, ,side of God and right he was not fulfilling all that New Tes- tament teaching required of hint, and be was not fulfilling that wise design which God had intended that he should have—the largest and best influence he was capable ef ex. eking among his fellow men. (Applause.) , Mr. WILLS, of Sunderland, also delivered an address and urged them to keep the intoxicating cup at a respectable distance. • . Mr. WILD, of Oldham, spoke of the influence they pos- sessed, and urged them to set a good example by signing the the pledge themselves and inducing others to do the same, (Applause.) Mr. J. KNOWLFS, of Lvmm, believed the intemperance of thiaconntry was wholly due to the professors of religion. (Applause.) He would not like to he one at it. He did not khow anything that was such a hindrance to the pregressof the Siinday schools as intempereoce, h e did not know any evil that took so many of their young people away from the Sunday school as intemperance did, nor did he know any- thing that kept AO many people 'from the house of God as intemperance did. If it was doing that, ought he to sup- port and encourage anything that tended to hinder what he thought was so desirable, and„what he was so anxious to attain? It looked to him like building up with one hand and pulling down with the other. He wanted them to employ both bands in one direction and that the right direction. (Applense.) Mr,Dvsote, of Oldham, said he saw the meeting was held under the auspices of the United Free Gospel Churches, and was very proud that it had been thought fit to conclude dne of the most successful conferences or annual meetings that be believed ever was held with a temperance meeting. He expressed his pleasure that the conference had recognised the temperance qtrestion, and had passed a resolution in regard to Bands of Hone; and remarked that he had very decided views on the temperance question, as he was thoroughly convinced it was the right question. Let them unite to promote total abstinence. His definition of tem- perance was total abstinence from all that was iniurious, and the moderate use of that which was useful and good. He was pleased to see that during the year the Connexional Committee-had sent out circulars to inquire into and plush on the Band of Hope work, and in conclusion urged them to give encouragement to the Band of Hope movement. (Ap- plause.) Votes of thanks having been accorded to the speakers and chairman, the meeting terminated. •

LO2D BEACONSFIELD AND R. • GLADSTONE. The following passage from the,latest sermon of the Rev Henry Ward Beecher which has 'reached this country, will be read with interest :—" Recently two great natures strug- gled for superiority in our mother land. One has gone, and the other holds the reins of empire over the grave. No generous heart loves to speak of faults ; but when you look at the moving ideas of Lord Beaconsfield and consider the, line of his literature, of his statesmanship, and of his inspiration, what new truth can you find that he discovered? What old truth htes he left burning brighter for his having lived ? What more heroic ideal did he in- corporate into life? What advance has human society made on account of what he did? What single quality did he make more resplendent, more noble, more desirable, for the whole human race? His is one of those names that, like a pyrotechnic display; burns brilliantly in the admira- tion of the crowd until the wheel ceases to revolve, and then goes out an is forgotten. He is finished ; his power is ended; and he has left nothing behind him tact a name—a ,name. But when he who stancls to-day so high in the ad- ministration of the forces ,of the Empire of Great Britain shall die;not alone will he have left behind him aflame and a work of scholarship and eloquent literature, but he will leave behind him RD example of courage for that which is I right, and of steadfast labour for advance in the quality of manhood; he will leave behind him the example of a Christian statesman seeking the best things by the highest 1 and purest ways; and if God 9hould spare his life, he will, I I think, carry his kingdom through those great transitions which threaten her so much, and which betoken the rise of I a better day; and of a higher morality and a nobler nationality. Until this heart ceases to beat I cannot separate myself from the desire, God bless our mother land. For ' her every stumbling and her every fault I have pain; for her every advance and, her every purification I have re- I joicing; and I both honour and revere that noble man who is a Christian statesman, and now stands prominent in the councils of the world. I know not such another. Not he of Germany ie to be compared with him; ani in my own land where is the man that equals him ? Of politicians we have enough; of nascent statesman we have enough ; but where is that man among 119 who embodies in himself the rovalty of Divine love combined with eminence and wisdom and skill in affairs? There is room for such a man here. May God send him to us speedily,"

div.head: 8 TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: 8 TRAVELS IN THE EAST.

alr A SOHTII-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [Sructat..] No. IV. NAPLES. Between Borne and Naples nothing remains fixed on the .uemory but the blazing out of the stars in the clear Italian aky, the rush of the train through dreary tunnels, across widely spreading fields and marshes, and beneath the shadow of dark mountains, as we perform the journey between the hours of eleven at night and six in the morn- ing. Naples was already astir. Its streets and quays nresented a scene of busy activity, as we drove this early to the western point of the bay. Nestling under its rocky promontory, the hotel commanded a delightful view of the due amphitheatre of mountain, city, and water. The island Of Capria, rising out of the deep blue sea, and seeming to recede or draw near just as the atmosphere was hazy or bright, became an object of deep interest through the day. When we came down from our ablutions we found the windows of the spacious saloon thrown wide open to admit the balmy air of that mid-February morning. and felt the change from our own dreary climate very agreeable. After a slight repast, we sallied forth to reconnoitre the city. Never, surely, was there such a city as Naples! For i comical contrasts and curious combinations, t beats all. Its velsicles are unique; a more strange and grotesque display of carriages and common street conveyances cannot be imagined. There they go, fastened, you scarcely know how, to ponies, asses, and oxen, and trundling along the to the crack of the hi bard smooth flagging to Sometimes you see an ass and a pony, sometimes an ass and an t)x and sometimes all three yoked together. And such poor, ill-fed beasts as they are, and se bedamed with brazan-trappings! And, worse for them, poor things, their owners seem to think their "go" should keen pace with their outward embellishments, rather than with the way they are furnished within. Itls_ no uncommon thing to see 15 or 20 full-

. _ gown people hanging on to one of these common Vetturino vehicles, as much in use in this neighboui hood. Then each strange burdens as are carried through the streets! Manure from the stable is heaped upon the back of the beasts in great loads; market produce of all kinds is carried in huge potties, wide at the top, pointed at the bottom and spreading out from the sides of the donkeys over half the roadway. The people seem exceedingly fond of street ex- hibitions. of Punch and Judy shows, and all sorts of theatrical entertainments. Outside of one of these shows it was amusing to et e a fellow lengthened out, by some process or other, to about eight feet high, and .nanufactured into the broadest possible caricature of a Romish priest, pacing to and fro amid the laughter and jeers of the onlookers. And this in Naples! The Stride Toledo is a scene of noisy fervid activity all day, and,! am told, nearly all night. The, streets leading into this great thoronghf are run steeply down the hill in parallel lines at short distances from each other, and, being all crowded with small shops, pour their busy population and traffic into 'it. Cab fares are exceedingly low, and hence a more varied commingling of rich and poor is perhaps nowhere to be seen. The most stylish of the gentry find themselves ever and anon palled up to allow fishwives, without caps or bonnets, to make their way in open cabs, in which they sit as much at their ease as the highest ladies in the land. But our time is short and we must make our way to a far different scene. The silent, ghostly streets of the disinterred Pompeii, as she sits, a skeleton in her opined grave, will very soon cool down the fever of bewilder nent created by her sister Napolis' too exuberant life and beauty. Whets sadness and deep solemnity creep over you as you look up the long and silent streets of that ill-fated, city, or stand within her theatres, squares, and temples. thrown open to the sun, after being for ages buried in darkness and dust! And, more- over, a trembling awe takes possession of the mind, and clings to it for days, when you realise the fact, as you must do by a faithful and unblinking examination, that, as surely as fire and brimstone came down out of heaven and des- troyed the cities of the plain for their crimes and sensuality, so surely did the burning ashes of Vesuvius consume this city for the crime cause. Row sudden and complete her destruction! Although thousands escaped, no less, we are told, than 600 bodies had beep dug out around which the ashes had formed a crust, and left an enduring mould. Several of these are now shown in the museum at the entrance. The figures are in various attitudes. One lady lies with jewels on her neck, and a ring visible on her finger ; another with her Min clinging to her bosom. There is also a poor dog, twisted together, as if writhing in its death agonies The ashes, as they fell in fiery clouds, were so scorching that not only were the lowest cellars filled up with it. hut the eyes 1 and mouth, and skulls of the skeletons stuffed with the all penetrating and devouring dust. Perhaps that which , came nearest to one's heart in cont,mplating the many ob- jects before us, were the evidences of the every-day life suddenly and for ever brought to a close. There was the month of a public fountain, in which was deeply indented the chafing of the bucket-rope all around its rim. The marks of drinking vessels were still to be seen on the marble counter of the wine shop. The heavy Roman pavement in the streets was worn into deep ruts by the carriages, similar to what we had seen in the Forum at Rome. The streets, —many of them are so narrow that two strides enable you to cross from one parapet to the other, and to facilitate this there are, at every few yards, big stone blocks in the cnitre of the streets, on a level with the side walks. Most of these are well worn with human feet. The chariots can never have been drawn by fewer than two horses, which must have run along in the spaces left on each side. These tokens of Pompeii's busy life at the moment of her destruc- tion are much more numerous in the relics which have been removed to the museum at Naples. Many paintings there are as fresh as if they had just been executed. There are sketches by school boys, advertisements, pictures of trades, &c. Then you have articles of every kind, from the child's toy to the key in the grasp of a skeleton's hand; you have pieces of money, tickets for admission to the theatre, &c. With saddened hearts, but instructed and admonished by what we had seen, we rode ha& from Pompeii to Naples. THE VOYAGE TO ALEXANDRIA.

Vesuvius had scarcely' been visible for weeks, but this morning, as we sailed out of the bay of Naples, every vol- tage of cloud and mist had disappeared, and it stood out against the bright blue sky in all its solemn majesty. The white smoke, as it rose from its summit, was resting in almost moveless folds in the clear atmosphere above. The bay itself, with its noble amphitheatre of water, surrounded by rocks and bills, and fringed with the city's varied out- line and busy shore, presented a scene of beauty never to be forgotten. The receding landscape, with Vesuvius as the central figure, occupied most of our attention during the afternoon. We were en board a French steamer, with a run of five. days before us, berths comfortable, waiters quiet and attentive, captain gentlemanly and obliging, everything moving onswith the regularity of clockwork. Well, how tihall I relate that, in spite of all these favefurable surround- ings, and with a sea as considerate of their stomachs as it reonld well be, some of our friends insisted on leaving the 4inner-table that flame evening, in order to pay their devo- tions to Neptune, and take his scaly tribes into their fellow- ship. As they did not repeat this curious performance more than once, I don't think I am called upon to mention names. I wanted to see *tromboli next morning, and was on deck by three o'clock. The vessel passed it at no great diatance, but the haze was so thick that we weir right oppo- site the island before the captain pointed it out to me as a dark object, scarcely visible, against the sky. I imagined I caught eight of a small glimmer of fire. When we came on dock at 7-30 the island was far away behind, with its single burning mountain rising out of the sea, from which along, long streak of smoke in a parallel line, with its horizon ex-* tended for miles. Between the classic rocks of Scyllea and Charybdis we , steered in all safety, neither running upon the one nor the other, and anchored in the harbour of Mes- sina about nine a.m. To those who bad just come away from the bleak skies and bitter blasts of our northern shores, the picture before us was indeed delightful. Boats were alongside, gently rolling about in the light blue crystal waves, with hundreds of floating sea-anemones arouid them, swarming with a wonderful instinct where food was likely to be forthcoming. The dark-eyed Italian boys were holding up the lich ripe oranges, with their beautiful green leaves still hanging to them, ready to roll them down at our feet three doer n fora shilling. One lame boy made his way on deck, and undertook to brush our boots. I never saw brushes fly from hand to hand, and round and round the foot, as that boy made them fly. Having four hours to wait we went on shore. Along the quay thousands of pipes of wine were spread for shipment. Flanked by a noble terrace of shops and houses, the guilty has a very •fine appearance from the large open harbour, two miles in circumferenc.e, in which the vessel cast anchor, and a very business- like air on shore. Our ramble through the prin- cipal streets was an enjoyment. Owing, perhaps, to the insulaticn of Messina, the costumes and general appearance of both men and women had a more truly national and primitive character than prevailed in most of the Italian cities we had visited. The almost Eastern eithplicity of their habits was seen at a public fountain, where several women in their quaint costumes and with their old fashioned ,pitchers were gathered. Each had brought a bamboo to reach from the spouts of the fountain to the neck of their pitchers, which were placed on the ledge ()Me large circu- lar basin surrounding the fountain. Slowly ran the water into th• vessels, affording the ladies time for the daily modicum ef gossip. Theis. lifting their pitchers to their ehoulders, eastern fashion, they bore them leisurely away. The manufacture of macaroni seems to be carried on chiefly by the poor people in Messina. We stood in an open spaCe at the head of the town, and watched some boys drying it in the sun. It was spread out on shallow frames with canvass bottom?, and the quickness of the boys in throwing the dried article from one end of the frame to the other, aud then throwing three or four into one, was something wonderful to behold. There was another retnarkable piece of meniputt- tion. We are accustomed to consider macaroni and vermicelli amongst the purest and cleanest of all our articles Cf diet. Will it be believed that, whenever one of those dirty looking boys saw that one of the soft tubes bad collapsed, he put it to his lips and blew it into shape again! As we steamed down the straits into the open sea, the motion of the yew!, as we sat at dinner, was scarcely perceptible. We had a fine view of Etna as we left it in the rear, and sailing closely into the toe of Italy, had a fair view of the land. The menuntains have a barren, sandy appearance, showing exeeedingly scant cultivation. My note book says: "While those at home are creeping over the fire in this chill Feb- ?nary eyeming, here we are under a bright blue sky, with

the sun shining so benignantly that a northeast wind has all the softness of a southern zephyr, and scarce inflates our sails es we pass into the open Mediterranean." Again at 9-30 p.m. "The weather is most delightful. We have paced the decks until we are wearied, and new we sit in the cabin, sipping our evening tea, with as little sense of motion as If we sat in our own room at home ; we can scarcely believe we are on the water." Monday morning, eight o'clock, saw us all sitting i on the deck watching the sland of Candle, about twenty miles away—the old Crete whose people "were always liars," but among whom the light of the Gospel sprung up under Paul's labours. In yonder island the beloved Titus I would receive and ponder. Paul's loving and faithful epistle. To what ate extent their former lives and present evil sur- roundings gave a bias and colouring to the Christian character and behaviour of the first disciples, the Pauline epistles but too clearly show. How natural and how neces- sary itvfas that the apostolic letters should take their tone and spirit, as well *5 their line of teaching and exhortation, from the peculiar circumstances of each church ! And what a labour it must have involved to study the condition and surroundings of each as they were affected by the various predominating vices and changing idolatries of the Pagan world! Eternity alone can declare to us all that Paul was and is to the Christian Church—all that Christ has wrought by this one man. We read that in ancient times, Crete was very prosperous and full of people. Homer in- dicates that in his time it contained a hundred cities. Under the teaching of its great legislator, Minos, the island gave laws even to Greece. But Crete derives its strongest interest from the fact that Paul was driven around this southern side of it, and took or sought shelter in two of its ports—Fair Havens, and Phenice—before he was wrecked on the island of Melita. We sailed much closer in to the small island of Claude, now called Gozzo, which stands quite as closely connected, in New Testament history, with Paul's memorable voyage as Crete. It is not more than seven miles long by three broad, but, according to Admiral Penrose, would afferd the advantage of a comparatively smooth sea for 12 or 15 miles, with the wind blowing even tempestuously from the north-east. The testimony of Luke is thit when they were sailing close in under the island of Crete, impelled by a soft eolith wind, suddenly the wind changed and a fierce tempest drove them away from under Crete round the east end of this little island, which lies to the south of Crete, where, keeping the vessel's head to the shore until they secured the boat and made all snug, they turned her round, fearing the quicksands, and, setting her sails to the wind were driven about in this very sea. More than 18 centuries had rolled away, and yet that one voyage, out of thousands of others, equally perilous, claimed our undivided thought! And why? Surely because the waters of the Mediterranean had never before or since borne upon its bosom so pure and magnanimous a soul as that which serenely gathered into itself in fullest sympathy and hopefulness, all the privations, horror, and distress of that despairing crew. The Picture is unique, almost unapproachable. The man that had lseen spurned and set at naught, stands forward now, their only hope in the hour of deepest nerd; bearing them all up in a fellowship of suffering that throws in its moral grandeur, the mightiest miracle working into the shade We cannot but believe that, if Paul, after the manner and in the power of his Divine Master, had said to the winds and waves "Peace, be still !" he would have enjoyed, in the sudden calm, an immediate immunity from suffering; but he chose to endure with his fellow passengers, that the image of Christ, in His sympathy with suffering might be re- vealed more fully in his person, and, though unconsciously that he might leave to us and to all Christians an example of true magnanimity and a ground of rejoicing that our common Christianity could produce such a man. (To be continued next week.)

div.head: THARSIS SULPHUR AND COPPE
div.p: THARSIS SULPHUR AND COPPE
COMPANY, LIMITED.

The annual meeting of the shareholders of the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Company (which has branches at Widnes, Glasgow, and other towns) was held on Wednes- day afternoon, in the Merchants' Hall, Glasgow; Mr. Chas. Tennant, M.P., presiding. The Secretary (Mr. Thomson) having read the notice calling the meeting, and the report having been held as read, the Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, said :—Our volume of business has been larger and more profitable than that of the previous year. Our deliveries of pyrites as well as production of copper have exceeded those of 1879. We have, moreover, added to our operations ths extraction of goll and silver by: the " Claudet " process, and which is now being carried out successfully at all our works. The prices we have obtained for enr iron ore and copper have been rather higher, but of sulphur the same as last year. We have had further the benefit of about £15,000 of profit on our share account, as detailed in the report, the total result being such as to war- rant our increasing our dividend to 25 per cent., after writing off more than usual and adding largely to our re- serve funds. The mines, both Tharsis and Calanas, now stand at only £340,000. " Miscellaneous assets," whicb,t.a you are aware, represented premiums and bonuses paid for certain riohts and patents acquired, and amounted originally to £20,000, have been written off entirely. The fictitious element, so to speak, has been eliminated, and our assets re- present now only real and tangible property. We have 188 shares g our own yet to dispose of, which will yield us a further considerable profit. The total extraction at Tharsis this year has been 318,583 tons, against 379,268 tons last year—a diminution of 80,885 tons; but last year left us with a stock in the depot at Tharsis of 89,220 tons, which is now reduced to 45,000 tens, in addition to our large stock of calcined ore. Our shipments have been 192,095 tons, as against 150,647 in 1879. I have an interesting fact to mention, viz., the discovery on our property of a consider- able deposit of cupreous schist, from which Mr. Grothe, by our ordinary cementation process, looks forward to obtain- ing a considerable supply of copper, At home the metal works have received more ample and regular supplies of cinders, and have gone on satisfactorily. The balance at the credit of profit and less account is £302,508 12s. ld., out of which we propose to pay 25 per cent, dividend, carrying. forward £18,344 12,1. 18. to the credit of the rent - rent year. The tripartite agreement has been renewed, and the price of sulphur continues at 81. for the current year, as well as for the years 1882, 1883, and 1884. We have sold OUL proportion for these periods, and trust thao we shall see such a general revival of business before long as will enable us to add to our respective quantities. Meantime our de- liveries to consumers for 1881 are not likely to fall short of those of last year. Of iron ore we have sold about half of our probable production at prices rather below those of last year. Copper, on which our profits mainly depend, shows some sign of improvement. I think that in counting on the average pricl. of last year we are not being too sanguine. Our establishments both in Spain and here are now very complete, and I look for at least as large and economical an. output from them as in the past year. The propriety of reducing our shares from £lO to some lower figures so as to bring them within the reach of small investors is engaging our attention. The details shall be laid before you in a special report, and ,we think you will find therein an accep- table solution of the £7 shares, and, at the sage time, a proposal which will be ad vantveous to the general interests of the company.—Mr. Alfred D. M. Meseeau seconded the adoption of the report, and it was put to the meeting and agreed to.—Mr. A. !Janney moved that the five directors who retire at this time—Messrs. John Moffat, Arch. Arrol, Jules barthelemy St. Hilaire, Alfred D. M. Messean, and M. V. Mercier—be re-elected.—Mr. Hugh Beckett seconded the motion, which was unanimously adopted.—M. Messeau thanked the shareholders for the bonour done his brother directors and himself in again electing them, and gave the assurance that they would continue to promote the interests of the company as far as lay in their ' power.—The auditors were re-appointed, and a vote a thanks having been accorded to the chairman, the meeting terminated.
