div.head: • THE EXAMINER, -SATURDAY, JUNE 25: 1881. WHY PAY RENT I
div.p: • THE EXAMINER, -SATURDAY, JUNE 25: 1881. WHY PAY RENT I

LECTURE BY MR. STARR, AT RUNCORN. The 405th Starr-Bowkett society having been commenced under promising auspices in Runcorn, on Wednesday even- ing, Mr. R. B. Starr (of London), the founder of these asso- ciations for mutual help, in conjunction with the late Dr. Bowkett, delivered a lecture in the Public Hall, in that town, on " Why Pay rent ?" to a very good audience, considering the fact of the gathering being in June. Mr. S. C. Beckett, trustee, presided, and there were on the platform Messrs. W. Armstrong, J. D. Jones, T. Booth, J. Wilson, Jabez Uns- worth, J. Barton, solicitor to the society; W. J. Davies. secretary; and Campbell, trustee. The CHAIRMAN said he had been requested, without any previous notice, to preside over the meeting, or he might have prepared a speech on the subject. However, they had with them that evening a star of the first magnitude, in the person of the lecturer—(hear, hear, and applause),—and, under the circumstances, it would, perhaps, hardly be ex- pected that he (the speaker) should say very much. Most of them, he believed, were aware that a Starr-Bowkett society was in course of formation for Runcorn and the dis- trict. He saw from various reports that similar societies had been exceedingly successful in London, Liverpool, and other cities; and, as the result of enquiries which he had made into the question, he had given in his name as one of the officers. He had not done this with the idea that it would be of much benefit to himself, but in the hope that the formation of such an association in the town would promote thrift amongst a considerable number of the population. He was of opinion that it would prove one of the best organisations for mutual help which they had amongst them, as the entrance fee was only Is., and the subscription sixpence per week for every £lOO. (Hear, hear, and applause.) In conclusion, he had pleasure in introeucing to them the lecturer. Mr. STARR hoped that they would give hirn that attention which was necessary in order that they might thoroughly grasp the chief principles of the society they were about to establish that night. The interesting ques- tions he should have to place before them in his lecture were—" Why pay rent?" and "How can I become my own landlord by the payment of a small weekly subscription? Some of those present might imagine that the Starr-Bow- kett building societies which were being formed up and , down the country were a new thing, but he must inform them that there were about 250 of them in London, and I many of them were 20 years old. The reason why the claims of such an organisation had not been brought before them in Runcorn many years ago was that a long time since he made up his mind not to go out of London, as it entailed such expense and logs of time. That scruple had, however, been got over, and he had disposed of a lucrative business in order that he might go thoroughly into the work of establishing these valuable building societies in the kingdom. He hoped that he might long be spared to carry on the work, as the associations were capable of doing such a large amount of good. He should speak to them of the great advantages of thrift, and then direct them to what he considered the best way of investing their money when they had saved it. He' dare say there were many people in the town, and a num- ber in that very meeting, who had never saved a penny all their lifetime, but who had never given a thought to the great claim which the landlord had upon their pockets for rent. He ventured to say that one-fourth of their earnings went in rent. Ile knew the case of a young man who said he could not pay for a share in their society, but his wife said he could if he would only give up his tobacco, which cost Is. 2d. a week. If he would give that up, she stated that she would add the other penny, and then he could take three shares, lie gave I it up and took three shares,. and in six years got his appro- priation and was then living in his own cottage, which he had named "Smoke Cottage." (Laughter.) Some of them I might have other ways of spending their money thought- lessly besides smoking or taking intoxicating drinks' and the question for them.to decide was whether they would give up some little luxury in order that they might save a little. They must not forget that their physical health and strength would decay, or younger men push them out of their situa- tions, and if they had not made some provision for their old age they would be in the position of many others, and have to say, "What an old fool I have been!" He regretted to say that many English people were not at all like the French in their habits of thrift. They would remember how wonderfully quick the French people paid the war indemnity demanded from them by the Germans. He had been in France and seen the French working men in summer evenings sitting outside some cafe, smoking very mild tobacco and sucking cheap wine through a quill, and the whole expense to them would be about threepence; but many of our working men would swallow threepenny- Worth of drink at one draught, and think nothing at all about it. (Laughter.) He wished they Could get all Eng- lish workingmen tie think these matters carefully over. After they had determined to save, there came the question of what was the hest thing for them to do with their money. He believed the best they could do with it was to invest it in some building Society; hut before they did so, he should always recommend them to learn what it would cost them to borrow ; secondly, how they would have to pay back what they had borrowed; and thirdly, what they would get fined if they did not pay. Many people decided that they should like to have a house, and they never stopped to con- sider what it would cost them, but rushed into a building society, and the fines and the repayments sometimes became no numerous. that, in the end, they wished they had never joined. He had never spoken one word against existing building societies, because, commercially speaking, they were just and proper. Bat the question arose of why workingmen were not members of them, for it was a fact that they seldom found them so. The first reason for this was that if a workingman wAnted to borrow £3OO, he would have to find a property worth at least £350, which in reality meant that he must find £5O. His connection with working people led him' to the conclusion that there were very few of them who could put their bands upon £5O, and, there- fore, they could not borrow from an ordinary building society. Even if a working man could find the £5O, he would have to pay the building society in interest on the principal £3OO for the 12i years as a rule, at /east £l5O, the total repayments being from £34 to £4O a year. A work- ingman bought a house worth £3OO only, and be had got to find the differsnce of £lO to £l4 a year. That was not within the relth of workingmen, or if so why did they not borrow of the interest societies? They were told to take a share, and so save their money until it became £5O. To take a share would cost 10e. a month. Where was the workingman who could pay halt-a-crown a week? He was defeated here again. Now his societies offered workingmen assistance, and he should be very much surprised if he did not mdablish without doubt that it was the cheapest and hest way for a man, who could not afford to pay interest, to get a house, in their rules they aimed at getting 500 members. The lecturer detailed the working of the meek* at length, the particulars, of avhich have appeared in these corumns before. If a member was out of work, or sick, there was no fine Hi- flicted. (Applause.) But he must not be sick ton often. (Laughter.) If a rnember,reported that he was out of work, or ill; and the Board of Management' found his statement to he correct, they had a discretionary power to remit all fines. .Though they had never yet sold a house from a working man, they had sold from some few speculative benders, where these worthies had got money which they had no right to have. He, however, supposed they had gilt net men of that kind in Rurfcorn. so he would say nothing flirther upon that point. , (Laughter.) If a working man took four shares, and after belonging to the society a year, he fell ill and could not pay his subscriptions, the board could advise him to lower the your shares to two, andlecanse he had paid on the four for the whale year. be would have nothing to paw on the two for the next twelve months. (Applause.) Mr. Starr argued that his seciety was not a mere commercial undertaking, but one deeply affecting social and domestic matters, and often leading to high morality. He must tell them, with deep regret, that many young women could not get a husband at all. (Laugh- ter.) Let them not laugh at that statement, at it was very bard. Why could they not? For a very good and substan- tial reason; as for every 100 women there were only 9ftmen. (Loud laughter.) He would undertake to say that as soon as any young woman got a ballot, she would have the power to selecting a husband from several candidates. (Laughter.) There had been 28 weddings in their societies within 23 months. (Laughter.) The lecturer gave several amusing illustrations of this paint. In 1848 the House of Commons held an inquiry as to why there was so much poverty and distress, and so men? men ' and women in the workhouses; and the result showed that three-fourths of the people in these places were there as the result of their own improvident habits. Let each man present if not married, take unto himself a wife, insane his life, and buy his own house. There were plenty of men in that neighbourhood who spent more than double the ex- pense per week required for a subscription to that eeciety, in beer. A man who had a family and paid 39. per week euhscription, could ultimately secure £6OO for his little ones. After some further explanations, the lecturer concluded by saving that he should have pleasure in replying to any question,' of a pertinent character. Two Warrington gentlemen then put several queetione. The chairman took the opinion of the meetine as to allowing these "impertinent questions," on which they decided that they shonlel not be continued, and the gentlemen had to leave the platform. The CHAIRMAN Raid it was quite evident that the Warrington men attended there to cause disorder ; and he should not allow Mr. Starr to be snubbed in the way he h.+d been that evening. Mr. R. FOULHFS said he had been much pleased with the ;.xplanation given by Mr. Starr, and he ceuld not see how it 1, they were careful in selecting good men as officers. and fel- -1 lowed out to their legitimate issue the principles upon which the societies were founded, they could come to grief in Rnneorn. The CHAIRMAN' said it appeared that Mr.Foulkee intended to make a speech. He could not allow him to do that—with an te,,rct—but be might ask any pertinent question. Mr. Foulkes then retired from the platform. ' Mr. CAMPRFLT„ manager to the Runcorn Soap and Alkali conei.h r. d that if the society were properly managed, it would mmt certainly prove successful. He inoi.),,,ed a vote of th inks to Mr. Starr. hnoolte.arnedal.col This was seconded by Mr. Pootn, of Weston, and carried with acclamation. reallyrepresento.” m men." Ware n The CHAIRMAN, in putting the resolution, took occasion to say be felt sure the two persons who bad interfered with the meeting ely did „ Mr. Smauw, in replying, said it was most unfair that, after rii,:toafirtrtn ovi, ttfmtthew

establishing a society, he should be blamed by a set of noodles if they happened to conduct it badly. He certainly intended that some of those who had been instrumental in injuring the Warrington society, which might have been made into a very good one, should hear from him again. The meeting then terminated.

I\-011THERN COUNTIES' CHAMPION- SHIP MEETING AT WIDNES. This long looked for meeting took place on Saturday, in the large field at Farnworth where the Widnes Athletic Club held their sports on the previous evening. The weather, which in the early part of the day had been of a rather gloomy character, brightened up in the afternoon, and there was an immense gathering of spectators. The officials under whose management the events took place were those connected with the Widnes club, and their names appeared in the last issue of The Examiner. Upwards of £2OO was taken in gate money. Few local athletes entered, as each race was for the championship, and each had to be started from the scratch. The entries this year numbered 174. against 500 last year. The races were capitally contested as a whole. The course was kept by a large body of police. THREE MILES' WALICING.—Iet H. Webster, Stoke V.A.C., 2nd J. Worrall, Livepool. Time, 22 minutes. Four en- tered. Last year Webster was rather heavily handicapped. and left the course after the ninth lap, but at this contest he appeared to have the race entirely in his own hands. In the tenth lap Webster passed Worrall, but only for a few yards, when the latter took the lead, but only to be passed in the next lap by his competitor, who put a consideraW distanc3 between them. This Webster gradually increased, and in the last lap he made a remarkably clever spurt, leaving Worrall about half slap to complete after he had passed the tape. THE BROAD JUMP.-ISI A. Summers, Stalybridge C.C., 20ft. lin ; 2nd P. Davin, Carrick-on-Suir A.C., 20ft. bin. There were eight entries, and, with one exception, all com- peted. Davin appeared to be a great favourite with the public, but he was beaten half an inch by A. Summers. 100 Yanns FLAT RACE.—let H. Chadwick, Rochdale , W.F.C., 2nd R. M. Massey London A.C. Time, 10 secs. This proved a very exciting race, as Chadwick and Massey it are both runners of note. Chadwick kept the lead through- out. _

HALF-MILE FLAT R4CE.-Ist R. Andrews, Stoke V.A.C., 2nd S. K. Holman, London A.C. Time 2 minutes 6 2-sth seconds. Great interest was shown in this race, in which six started, as R. W. Whalley, a local man, who beat all corners, including some London Men, in the scratch mile, was competing. Whalley ran well, but lost all his chance of winning at the commencement of the last lap, and drew out. Holman, the London runner, disappointed the hopes of his supporters, as he only took second place. Andrews, who is a magnificent runner, went to the tape a winner by four yards. The contest for the second and third place was a very keen one. , Gvanagrlcs.-Ist G. W. Renshaw, Haslingden, 2nd Philip North, Bradford. Renshaw's work en the bars called I forth loud applause. QUARTER-MILE FLAT RACE.-Ist F. W. Schofield, Wigan C.C., 2nd W. Nugent. Time. 55 seconds. Only the two winners started. Schofield took the lead until he came to the passing of one of the corners, when Nugent, who was making a terrible rush for first place, cannoned with him. Schofield retaliated by pushing Nugent forward with his hands, and after running a few yards further, he gave up. The tele' showed Nugent fist and Schofield secorid, but the latter handed in his ohj.ction, and the judges decided that Nugent had thrown himself out, and gave the first prize to Schofield. When, however, at the close et the pro- ceedings, Schofield went up to receive the gold medal, those whoconsidered he had not won it, and who probably had not noticed the cinnoning above referred to, were loud hi their expressions of dissatisfaction, and did a considerable amount of groaning. On this taking place, Mr. Gossage, the president of the club, said the grumblers had no right to express their feelings in such a manner, as the power of de- ciding as to the various events rested exclusively with the judges. HIGH JllMP.—lett P. Davin, 2nd 1). H. Brownfield. Height, sft. Sin. Davin won easily. ONE MILE FLAT RACIL—Ist, William Snook, Moseley Harriers, 2ad E. Wright, Widnes F.C. Timer 4 minutes 41 3-5 seconds. Snook is a splendid runner, and caused much amusement to the spectators by the manner in which he coquetted with his opponents. He allowed Wright to take the lead for some laps but kept close upon his heels, Fox, of Claughton, and Hoimaa meanwhile running together several yards behind, but being simply nowhere in the race. In the third lap Wright, having forged ahead, managed to keep his position well, and was loudly cheered by the people belonging to the immediate neighbourhood. Snook broke the tape at his leisure, 'with several yards to the

good. ONE MILE BICYCLE Rees.-18t F. Clarke, Moston, 2nd J. E. Tolson, Huddersfield. In this race four started. W. Smith. of Widnes, at once took first place, being followed very closely lay Hutchin, who managed' to get first in the second round. Clarke made a spurt, and compelled Hut- chin to take the next place. At this stage Smith lost a shoe, and gave up running when he had three laps to finish. Hutchin kept close to Clarke, but finally Tolson drew up and spoiled Hutchin's chance of getting second place. PUTTING THE SHOT (181b5).-Ist Geo. Ross, Patricroft, 2nd P. David. ' Distance 40 feet 9 inches. THREE-QUARTEH MILE STEEPLECHASE.—Ist T. Crellin, 2nd T. Concannon. Time 3, minutes 57 4-5 seconds. Four started, and the number of hurdles, surmounted with furze, and followed by a water jump, was the same. Schofield at one fine leap cleared the water jump, whilst each of his op- ponents alighted in the watery element. He also cleared the water a second time, amidst the loud cheers of the spec- tators, hut retired after jumping the next hurdle. Concan- non made a desperate effort to catch Crellip, but had not the ghost of a chance. 120 YARDS HURDLE RACE.—let F. F. Cleaver, Notts Forest C.C., 2nd P. Davin, Carrick-on-Suir A.G. Time, 16 4-5 seconds. Only three started. Balmer, of Rock Ferry, had no chance, and the other two men jumped the hurdles together, Cleaver just succeeding in breasting the tape a yard or two before Davin. PO= JUMp.--lst Tom Ray, Ulverston, 2nd E. A. Stra- chan, Preston. These were the only two competitors. Ray last year cleared 11 feet and carried off the first prize, clear- ing 11 feet 2i inches' apparently very easily-. FIVE II7ILES Bieseis RACE.-ISt J. E. Tolson, Hudders- . field, 2nd F. Clarke, Moston. Time 19 minutes 581-5 Skli. This was a magnificent race. ,Clarke at once went to the front, closely followed by Tolson. Hutchin was third, and Ansdell was a good fourth, bat the latter only went round about threedaps, when he gave up. Hutchin ultimately retired from the contest. The renfaining men had then 19 laps to finish. For two laps Clarke kept the first place, when, amidst - enthusiastic cheering, Tolson went to the front at a terrific pace. Clarke, however, passed him in tile next lap. After a few more rounds Tolson passed his man, amidst great cheering, on the home length. Two Mrrans FLAT RActe—lst W. Snook, Moseley Har- rierS, 21md E, Wright, Widnes F.C. In the last four laps Snook literallY.ran away from his man. The issue of this race was never for a moment in doubt, and when Snook had finished the distance Wriget had still three-quarters of a lap te complete: This completed the events, ane the prizes were distributed at the grand stand by Dr. Booth. The following appeared in The Athletic News concerning ' these sports :—"r am sorry that I cannot compliment the Northern Counties Athletic Association on the unqualified success of their meeting on Saturday at Widnes. There were plenty of events, and, in most cases the entries were large,tr as large as could he expected at a meeting where there were nethint: bet scratch contests, but somehow the events did not go off with that " fizz" that was anticipated: The absence of Phillips. George, Myers, and Merrill took a lot of the interest away from the meeting, and the action of the London Athletic Club•authorities in persuading the Ainericens to withdraw from the Northern Counties Meet- ing, so that they could make their first appearance in Eng- land at- the London A.C. Meeting, was much discussed." LS.

There has been another attempt to upset a train on the Lancashire awl Yorkshire Railway. As a platdayer was walking along the Harwich branch linehediscoveied several pieces of iron lying on the metals not far from the level crossing between Sharrock's Pnd Hilton's farms. A train Passed ever the spot a short time afterwards. The police are investigating the matter.

- THRUM TO ALCMp iIAjOB GRIM'S HOUSS.—A young man named Joseph Laing was prosecuted at the Liver- pool Police Court on Tuesday for very singuloe conduct. On Monday night Laing went to Major Greig's house in Rodney- -51., Liverpool, in a state of intoxication; declared that he had come to give "special information"; and made some in- coherent remarks about blowing up the chief constable's house. Be behaved very outrageously.; and when taken into custody declared that "it he could not do it, his chums would." There was probably nothing in all this talk but the muddled mysteriousness of a stupidly drunken man, and il,,,tajor Grieg very kindly interceded with the bench on the prisoner's behalf. But the magistrates declined to over- look the assault on the constables, and fined the man 40s. and costs, with the alternative of a mates imprisonment. Stich escapades as this often, become contvrious, and the bench exercised a wise discretion in taking a serious view of the ease.

div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthlf meeting was held on Thursday. Mr. T. Button-Thnmis, vresided, and there were also present the Revs. George Holit;way, and Thomas Finegan; Messrs. Brock, Davis, O'Keeffe,, Shaw, and Denby, clerk.

RxTRAcsatdiSARY Previous to the ordinary busies, an extraordinary meet- ing was held for the purpose oi supplying the vacancy caused by the disqualification of Mr.. Martin Taylor.—The CHAIRMAN said he thought he ought, in the first place, to explain that he had recaived a letter from a gentleman whose name he had forgotten, but he believed it was Mr. Owens, suggesting, as a representative of the Noncon- formists, that Mr. Stringer should be elected to the position. It was within the knowledge of the members that Mr. Martin Taylor was a Nonconformist; and, therefore, it was only right and fair that the members of that religious section of the community should elect one in his place. Since receiv- ing that letter, be had been told that Mr. Wm. Hartland, who was a very prominent member of the Nonconformist body in Whines—and he P•ought none was more respected—had ex- pressed his willingness to return to the Board. They were all aware that when Mr. Hartland was amongst them, he rendered them very great assistance, and so long as he was willing to serve them again, it was a question whether they should not make use of his experience rather than elect a gentleman as member who was new to the work. Mr. Hartland always worked very harmoniously with all the gentlemen upon the Board, and he was, personally, of opinion that they would he serving the township by re-electing him; but he was en- tirely in the hands of his fellow members. He now left the matter with them to make any nomination they pleased.— Mr. Broca had great pleasure in proposing that Mr. Wm. Hartland he elected to serve in the room of Mr. Martin Taylor. He had worked with Mr. Hartland for many years, during which he was a memb.r of the Sites and Buildings Committee, and they al ways acted together most harmoniously That gentleman was also possessed of a good deal of informa- tion with regard to the work ef the School Board, having had a good deal of experience, which could all be utilised, in connection with it. —Mr. Suaw, in seconding the motion, said he had intended to submit the name of another gentleman to the members, but seeing that they s.emed to be unanimous in their desire to elect a gentleman, for the remainder of the term for which they had to sit, who had large experience, he did not think he could do better than fall in with their viewi. If Mr. Brock had not pro- posed Mr. Hartland, he (the speaker) should have done so, under the circumstances. He had pleasure in seconding the proposition, believing as he did that Mr. Hartland would be willing, as he had done in the past, to do the bat he could for the advancement of the educational work of the town.— The Rev. T. Thracian said be should 'be OM to see Mr. Hartland amongst them once more.—The.proposition was carried nen, die.; and afterwards, Coe CHAIRMAN said ha felt sure that the name`ef Mr. Hartland would be acceptable to that section of the population of Wickes, With which be was so intimately associated. MrUartland. bathe entire con- fidence of that part of the community; and he also believed that the working classes, as a body, would be glad to have I him back again on the Board, as they had every faith in him. He did not believe that Mr. Hartland had really any wish to be upon the Board again, but he had agreed to accept the ^flice, if elected, because it had been represented to him that would be for the good of the ratepayers he should do so. The following minutes were pissed : DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

This committee's report showed that during May the number of cases summoned before them had been 399, of which 10G bad been applications for contravention of the ;ducation Act. Fees were recommended to be paid In 84 cages. Twenty-two of the applications for fees had been re- fused. The number of prosecutions before the magistrates had been 11, and there had been an equal number of con victions. Two children had been sent to industrial schools.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

This committee recommended that accounts amounting to £377 9s. lid. should be paid. Since the last report £023 had been paid into the bank; and amongst the items were £5OO from the rating authority and 38. 11d, books sold to cbil dren.

HOLIDAYS. The following motion was passed, after the Rev. Thomas Finegan had suggested the adoption of another course as to the time when holidays should be taken another year : "That in order to meet the convenience of members of the Board who wish to be away during the summer months, regulation Bbe sampended, so as to allow.of the ordinary meetings of the Board being held in July on the first Thurs- day in the month, and in August on the last."

THE PRIVACY OF THE CENSUS RETURNS. The CLERK read the following communications which had been received in reply to applications from the Board for certain educational statistics—referred to in our last report —which it was suggested might be obtained from the cen- sus returns :—"Education Department, 3 June, 1881.—Sir. —I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of the memorial of your Board, dated 26th ult. An application similar to that which you have submitted in the form of a memorial from the School Board of Widnes, was submitted to the Local Government Board, in June last, and my lords were informed by the Department that there were serious objections which must preclude them from acceding to it.— I have the honour to he, sir, your obedt. servant P. Cuntrr." —" Census Office, Craig's Court, Charing Crnss, 30th May, I 1881—Sir,—In reply to your letter of the 26th instant, I am directed by the Registrar-General to inform you that he regrets heir; unable to =ably with your request, as there are, in his opinion, very grave objections to tnaking the census documents available for educational purposes, and it is distinctly laid down that the contents of the householders' schedules will be treated coufidentialjv.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, J. F. WiLiums, secretary."—The RATR- MAN It Seems 10 be a slight hit of red-tapeism.—Dr. 'O'KEEFE (Home Ruler) : I think that it would have been better for them to give them to 119 rather than let the police authorities make use of them against the tenants. (Laugh- ter.)—The birsrustats (hurnourouely) : That is hardly be- fore us, Dr. O'Keeffe. (Renewed laughter).—The proceed- ings then terminated.

div.p: WIDNES POLICE 'COURT. WasniasDAY.---Before Mr. W. N. Heald (Oalrrnan) and Mr. F. H. Gossage.

Fiawrirm IN THE STREST.—Tholnag Concannon was sum- moned for committing a bleach of the peace by fighting with Patrick Kelly.—P.C. Stricklansi said that on the 7th inst. he saw defendant fighting withriKelly in Tanhouse- lane.—Defendant was ordered to be bound over, himself in one surety of £lO and two in £5, to keep the peace for one month, or, in default, be sent to gaol 14 days. AN UNHAPPY EARL! MAE:RIAGE.—A stonemason named Roberts was summoued by his wife Jane for assaulting her. Complainant is 23 years old and defendant one year younger, and she stated that on the 17th inst. he attacked her witteaut provocation.—Defendant said his wife had irritated him by calling him names.—The Chairman remarked that the assault defendant had committed upon "the poor girl" who was his, wife was a most cowardly one. He ought to be ashamed of himself, and would be ordered to enter into sureties to keep the peace six months, himself in LW and two in £5. Bmwo Ore. PIECE or a WOMAN'S EAR.---Ann Quinn, a neatly-dressed woman, who had been apprehended on a warrant, was charged with unlawfully wounding Sarah Owens.—Complainant stated that for various reasons she should prefer, to withdraw from the case.-111r. Lewin, deputy.town clerk, said the statement made by the woman when she applied for a warrant apparently showed that the prisoner had been guilty of a most brutal assault. The question for the magistrates to consider was whether they mould permit complainant to withdraw from the case. The Bench said they should not do so; and Owens then said that she was the wife of Thomas Owens, of 34, Oxford-street and the prisoner lived next door to her. On Monday, the 20th inst., prisoner came to her door about a quarter to five o'clock in the afternoon, and asked her to take her little child out of tlke street, at the same time calling it a very foul name. She told the prisoner that she could not beat sense int° her child, and she then went out to take it in. Quinn seized her by the hair, and dragged her into prisoner's house, after which she beat her about the head with her fists in a shameful manner, and bit through her ear. During the time of the assault, prisoner held hereicross a chair. She lost a qnantity of blood, and had suffered great pain from the wound. After Quinn had bitten her, she remarked that she was not the first whom she had served in the same manner. Witness remained about half an hour in the prisoner's house, as she was unable to move through weakness. She then went to the police station and MR the' inspector, who sent her to Dr. Cooper, and she bad the wound dressed by his assistant. The woman bit the earring completely out of her ear, and the mark on that article of jewellery, which she now produced in court, was caused by her teeth. Witneee had not been able to sleep since. She did not wish to give evidence against the prisoner, though she had assaulted her without any provocation. Prisoner had had "a drop of,drink " at the time, or she did not suppose- she would have done such a thing.—Quinn said' that the complainant challenged her out to fight first, and as she bad a poker in her hand, she dragged her into the house and took it from her.—ln reply to the prisoner, complainant said she had never known her to bite anyone before, although she had heard of her Once biting a girt.—Sergeant Robinson proved apprehending the prisoner that morning, and charged her with the offence, on which she 'mid it was net true that she hit the prisoner.—Dr. Cooper said he had examined the wound in the ear, which was, even then, in avery inflamed state. There were two cute On the ear, which appeared to have been caused by two distinct bites. Complainant was ,still suffering great ptin.—Prigoner was then formally charged: She denied having bitten the complainant, and mid the wound in complainant's ear must have been caused whilst he was struggling with her for the *possession of the noker.—Prisoner was then committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial, and the ntaistratea agreed to ac- cept bail, herself in £2O and two in £lO. OFFERING TO 1111 Y A WONIAN A SET OF FALSE TEEM— Peter Finn was summoned for assaulting Margaret Kennedy. —Complainant said she was standing at her door.when the defendant came up, and teased her about 21-d. whiah he had in his hand. On ordering him away he knocked her down, —A witness was called for the dofence, who said the defen- dant annoyed the complainant by pronlising to buy her a S set of false teeth if she would only keep her tongue still. Complainant struck the man twice before,he did anything ` to her. If she had not known the woman be conduct Was snch that she should have supposed she AS an escaped lunatic.—The summons was dismissed.

div.head: RUNCORN PODICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN PODICE COURT.

Morrner.—Before Mr. William Banes (chairman) atul Mr. Alfred Thomas. A WARRINGTON MAGISTRATE SIIMMONED.—Mr. Edward Milner, J.P., of Warrington. was summoned by Mr. James Farrington, inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Au- thority, for having, on the 3rd inst., at Preston-o'th'-Hill, used a boat on the B idgewater Canal without having it lettered, marked, and numbered, in accordance with the Canal Boats' Act.—The Inspector said that on the 26th March he saw the defendant's boat in the township of Preston-o'-th'-Hill, and it was not lettered, marked, or numbered, as required by the Act. He told the defendant's man about the matter, . but on the 3rd June k e saw the . .
same vessel and found that it bad not even then been put in - • • • • • •- -

proper condition.—A gentleman appeared on behalf Of de- fendant, who handed certain documents to the Bench, after which the Chairman said it clearly appeared from the papers placed before the magistrates that the vessel had not been marked and numbered owing to the necessary certifi- _ _ . - . . -
cate Rot having been received from the Leigh Local Board. At the same time, the magistrates had no option but to en fore the Act, and defendant would have to pay 6d. fine
and 13s. costs.

SUMMONS AGAINST A LATE RUNCORN BOOLSELLEB.— Mr. Benjamin Simner, lately of Canada, formerly carrying on business in Bridge-street, (under the title of Messrs. Jones and Co.), as a bookseller, was summoned by Mr. Nixon, assistant overseer' for non-payment of poor rate amounting to £1 15s. sd. Defendant's wife admitted that she had possession of the key of the house, which is situated at Halton Brook, although she left it on the 9th inst. Her husband was ill in Wales, and she was also living there at present.—The Bench made an order upon defendant to pay the amount of the rate and ss. costs.—Mrs, Simner, who ap-
peared much moved, said she was in considerable trouble at present, and hoped the magistrates would grant her time in which to pay the money.—The Chairman said she would be allowed a month.

THY CAT AMOVGST THN PIOEONS.—James Gayter, powerful looking men, was summoned for assaulting Thomas Turfey on the 11th inst.—Complainant said he was going home after having been at the Navigation Inn, when the defendant, who had for a long time been one of his neigh- bours, met him, and asked him if his cat had been in his (defendant's) pigeon-cote and stolen a pigeon. He replied that he did not know, on which defendant pulled his coat off and wanted to fight. He declined to have anything to do with him, on which defendant's wife came up and followed him to his door, " blackguarding him" all the way. He put his hand up to push the woman from him, when defendant's son struck him. He afterwards got

away, but sotne short time following the defendant saw him and commenced another row, in which he (defendant) struck him, and a policeman had to be sent for. —Defendant, in reply to the Bench, said that all he said to the complainant near the Navigation Inn, ,was to tell him . .
that his cat had killed one of his pigeons, which_ he would not have sold for 20a., and ask

him whether he would make him compensation or destroy pussy.—Joseph Wilkinson was called for the defence, and said there was a great row caused in the street by the com- plainant the same evening, before the defendant had come home. Complainant shuck defendant's sons, and his wife and daughter.—Mary Ann Wilkinson, Spring *atdens, said she saw complainant hit Mrs. Gayter in the breast —The Bench said there appeared to be a doubt in the case, and the summons would be dismissed. .Tnn SALVATION ARMY IN COIIRT.—A HINT 'TO HOUGHS. —Robert Cowman, a young man, was summoned for having assaulted Mr. Jonas Inman, captain of the branch of the Sal- vation Army in Runcorn, and Mrs. Ann Washburn, Granville- street, on the 12th inst.—The complainant said that in the evening in question he was leading the Salvation procession through the streets to the Public Hall, and when near that building the defendant, with a number of other men, did all they could to break up their ranks. Previous to arriving in Church-street, the defendant and a number of other , young men had been annoying them by forming an opposi- tion procession and singing satirical hymns of their own composition, with the object of making fun. When near the Public Hall defendant and his friends tried to break their rinks, and witness did his best to prevent this, on which the defendant's company pushed him, and, just as he was turning round, Cowman hit him on the left cheek.— Defendant: All that I can say is that he snuck me just as he was turning round.—Matthevr John Sweetman, Heath- road, stated that he followed the procession down the town, and kept between the outsiders an/ the army. When they came to the st-est leading to the Public Hall a great 'lush took place on the ranks, and as Captain Inman turned round to get past, defendant struck him. He did not see the cap- tain strike Cowman.—Defendant: I know that I struck him after he etrucirme.—Shadrack Jones, a Weston young man, said that a rrember of young fellows accompanied the army detachment frown Mill-brow to the Public Hall, singing songs of their own making. When near the building the roughs broke the ranks and the defendant struck the captain on the left cheek.—By the Chairman: Did the captain wave his hand at all at the time of the alleged assault? No.—Did the captain go against the prisoner when he turned round? No • the defendant was two or three men behind the captain at No; time, and he pressed forward and delivered the blow. —By defendant: It took place between the committee room door, of the Co-operative Hall and the Public Hall door.— Mrs. Mary Ellison said she left, her house about half-past five to go to the men who were in pocession on Heath-road, and when she got near them she could not tell who were singing loudest, the group of noisy young men who accom- panied the procession to disturb it, or those of the Salvation Army. The rough young ftllows shouted down the singers of the army, who then formed eight deep, for the purpose of walking to the Public Hail. As soon as the army started a hymn the young men, who had formed themselves into a company, commenced another, and walked with them down to the entrance to the street in which the Public Hall is situate. The roughs then pushed into their rants, and. Sister Washburn forced some boys away from- the army. As soon as she lied done this defendant gave her a blow on the cheek, knocking the , skin off the bone. When the captain saw this, he came from the spot where he was standing, and tried to keep-the young men away from the procession. In doing this he re- ceived a blow over the, eye. Witness said that if the men hit anyone, they must strike her and the other sisters on stating which, she was given a blow on the eye. Defendant told Mrs. Washburn he woLld knock her spectacles off, Mad used had language. It was not true that Captain Inman struck defendant. —Mrs. Ann Washburn, an elderly and very respectable looking women, of Granville-street, said that on the evening of the lfith, the army were marching from Mill Brow, when a company of young men began to assault them, and continued to do so until they got into Church-street. ,There They made an attempt to break into the ranks by pushing a number of' fads amongst them. In order to get along she pushed the boys back, on which the defendant gave her a blow on her left cheek, and knocked. off her spectacles.. But for the great presence of the crowd- she would have fallen.—D4endant : I never saw this woman at all that Suraday evening.—A woman named Mary Ellis, said she was close to Mrs. Washburn when the, defendant struqk her. She stood forward to prevent her getting another blow, and received one herself on the right eye.— Samuel Edwards was called for the defence, and appeared tee have great difficulty in articulating his words co as to be understood.—Superintendent Williamson (to the witneas, who appeared to be chewing his cud): You have got some- thing in your mouth which you had better pull out before giving your ' evidence.—Witness then pulled out what appeared to be a quid of tobacco,,aald dropped it very sheepishly into the witness box. He went on to say that the disturbance arose owing to Captain Inman pushing the people, who were on the parapet near the Public Hall. He saw the captain hit CoWman on the jaw, whilst he (defen- dant) was standing on the parapet —By Capt tin Intim : Were not you leading the procession who were singing- against us P—No ; there were a lot before me.—The Chair- man (to witness): Were you one.—Yes; I was one walking alongside defendant. We were singing hyrens.—A witness named Antrohus, who lives in Nelson-street, said that at the time of the assault there were "a whole drove, consiet- ing, of 500 or 600 on the parapet." Mrs. Washburn and the captain commenced to push them before they could get round the corner of the street leading to the Public Han. Mr. Inman strUck at Cowman, on which the latter returned the blow, but he did not strike Mrs. Washburn.—By Mr. Hankes : Were you in the procession? Ye.—Which? In my own. (Laughter.)—What were you doing there? We were going into the Public Hall with them.—To annoy them, I suppose. Now, what were von singing? The other witness said you were singing. Nialiat was it? "I'm glad that I'm converted"! (Laughter.) I should think that we had as much right to sing as we went through the 'streets RS they had !—A young man named-Peacock was next called for the defence, and said he saw Captain Inman strike the defendant under the neck.—Mr. Bankes to the Superinten- dent f There is nothing against the defendant before, I sup- pose P--Superintendent Williamson: Not against this one individual ; but I intended to say a few words after your worships had decided the case. I may, perhaps, make the remarks now. The Salvation Aimv have now been in the town eomething like three years; and during the whole of that time they have conducted,their processions in a. very orderly manner. In fact, I feel proud that they are in the town, for they have done a considerable amount of good in Runcorn : and they are deserving of protection ins long as they conduct their proeessionn in a proper mar.ner. During the last few weeks, whilst the members of the army have been walking throngh the streets, I have observed a number of young men walking on the opposite side of- them mid singing some hymn of a satirical nature.—The Chairman No doubt to antoy them.—The Superintendent: I should like it to go forth to these young men and others, that the Salvation Army will be protected as long as they conduct their proceedings in an orderly manner.—The Chairman (to I defendant): It is quite clear to the Bench, that you com- mitted the assault in both canes, and you will be: fined 58.1 and coats in each case.—The costs in the first case were e 16e. 6d., and in the second 10s. 6d. The decision of th Bench was received with some slight applause, which w,„: immediately suppressed. IMPORTANT ANNOUNCEMENT.' DERKIN'S BEACH CONSOLS (Limited).--Since the appearance of the preliminary advertisement of this Com- pany, issued on the eve of Important operations at the Mine, we are now able to make the announcement that "The Cheat Spar Lode." which proved so enormously rich in the upper levels, has been opened upon in the Deep Adit Level. Important communication from Captain Ridge, June 9th," I beg to inform you 'The Great Spar Lode' we are driving upon East at the Deep Adlt Level is improving in width, a good strong kindly lode." Juhe 16th. "We are making good pro- gress in driving East upon The Great Spar Lde,' and in about five or six fathoms further I expect we shall cross ' The Pump Lump Lode,' where it forms a junction with 'The Great Spar, Lode'" " The Great Spar Lode " is strong and kindly composed prin- cipally of white eivan and lime spar, similar iu character to Bnailbeach and Tankerville Mines.

THE PROFIT SHOPKEEPERS. . • The class of Tradesmen who have been hap- pily de ignated Big Profit Shopkeepers are to be found in every town in the ki gdom. It Is so much easier to do a small Butane's at a Big Profit than a large one at a Small Profit. There is not half the work about it. A very few customers in the course of the day suffices to make a comfortable income. The People's Pockets suffer in consequence. Recognizing this fact the GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY was formed a few years ago to supply direct to the Public CLOTHING at the WHOLESALE PRICES. The Company have extensive works at which they manufac- ture every garment they sell. Whenever they open a Branch Business the Big Profit Shop- keepers are hugely alarmed; ni there is no love lost between the Grand Clothing Hall Company and the Big Profit Shopkeepers. But the Public believe in the Grand Clothing Hall Company. It b, comes a consideration when they can purchases Boy's Suit at 4s. 6d.. when for the same suit the Big Profit Shop- keepers require is. ed.; or a Gentleman's Suit to measure for 425. for which the Big Profit Shopkeepers require 555. The Big Profit Shopkeepers are very worthy persons, but they are so hampered with the Tally Credit, System that although they may copy the Grand Clothing Hall Company's windows, and other advertisements, they cannot do with Small Profits, hence they are so bitter against THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY BRIDGE STREET, WARRINGTON.

NEWTON, RAYDOCS, AND GOLRORNE PERMANENT BENE- FIT BUILDING CLUB.-The annual meeting of this society Was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Friday. Mr. T:',J, Gillespie, one of the trustees, presided. The working on the year it will be seen from the following particulars heel not been so successful as former years, the society this year, for the first time, only paying a dividend of 41 per cent.' Although the managers had tO limit the issue of invested. shares, there has been received under this head £3,562 10s. Bd., and the amount now standing to the credit sf the mem- bers is £55,172 4s. 10d., which is £204 Is. 2d. less than at ' the issue of last report. There has been advanced during the year £6,860 Bs. Id., and the repaypaents qadvances amount to £6,664 Os. 2d2 The aunt now outstanding on the Mort- gage security of 79 lots of property belonging to 61 borrow- ing members, is £59,554 us. 7d., being £196 7s. 11d., more than at last report. The net profits for the year amount to £2,636 2s. 5d., which the managers have decided to deal with as follows :-Te pay a dividend at the rate of 4it per cent, per annum, which will absorb £2,434 4s. 104., and to carry forward to the reserve fund £2Ol. 178. 7d, which will increase that fund to £2,804 3s. 4d., and which is equal to 5 per cent. on the total amount standing to the credit of the members. The managers consider it more prudent in these depressed times, and keeping in view the large depreciation in the value of all properties, to strengthen the resarve fund 'rather than to pay a higher rate of dividend. The society consists of 623 members holding 5,542 invested shares, and 6,584 purchased shares, being an increase for the year ot seven members. Tbe auditor was Mr. F. Lambert Stevens. The officers for the past year were re-elected, and a vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings. Scnoors TREATS ON RACE THIIRSDAY.-The annual treat to the Wesleyan Sunday school scholars was given on' race Thursday. The Children, headed by a band, paraded the main streets, and proceeded to Mr. Kilahaw's fiele at Burtpp- wood. The youngest children were conveyed in treverai large waggons, which had been kind y lent by Mr. Emmett, of the London and North-Western waggon works. The afternoon was spent in innocent games, romping; eke.' A bountiful supply of refreshments were supplied to the children. The Baptist, Primitive Methodists, and Ragged schoels combined, and gave a similar treat to the scholars attending their Sunday schools. The weather was beauti- ful and the day heartily enjoyed by both teachers, scholars, and friends. ..

Valuable FREEHOLD RESIDENCES, FARMS, and Small Holdings at M OBBERLST, NEAR KNUTBFO6D, in the County of Chester, within 12 miles from Manchester.—TO BE SOLD BY AUCTION by order of the Executors of the late J.
